```text
  Not memory estimation by itself. The new thing is making `.estimate` a planner
  and admission contract that predicts which storage profile can run under a
  budget, then proving after the run whether that contract held.

Why care about fictitious graph estimates?
  They let users ask "could this enormous graph fit?" before loading it. That is
  exactly the PMF shape for budget-bounded batch compute.

What must Knight Bus avoid?
  Returning a smaller byte number without schema parity, graph+algorithm
  separation, large-dimension tests, or runtime proof. That would be less
  trustworthy than GDS, not more.
```

The pass-087 product decision:

```text
Build the first estimate API before the first heroic hot loop.
Make it schema-compatible enough to feel familiar, but stronger by adding:
  cap
  admitted profile
  profile alternatives
  large-graph fixture coverage
  measured high-water receipt link
```

#### GDS Memory Trees Give Us The Accounting Algebra

Pass 088 adds a subtle but important lesson: the estimate result is not only a
row schema. Under it is a tree-shaped accounting model.

GDS has two accounting operators that matter for Knight Bus:

| Accounting Shape | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Use |
|---|---|---|
| Additive resident tree | `CompositeTree.memoryUsage` sums child ranges | graph projection + algorithm state + output state that are resident together |
| Max/high-water tree | `CompositeMaxTree.memoryUsage` takes max child range | sequential phases, profile alternatives, spill pipelines, and "only one frontier slab at a time" profiles |
| Range arithmetic | `MemoryRange` carries `min` and `max` and uses exact arithmetic | uncertainty bands, large-dimension overflow guards, and cap admission |
| Human render | `MemoryTree.render` and `Estimate.humanReadable` | familiar `.estimate` UX |
| Machine render | `MemoryTree.renderMap` with `name`, `memoryUsage`, `components` | LLM-readable, testable receipt structure |

This changes how we should design low-RAM estimates. A flat "bytes required"
number is too blunt. The estimate should be a proof-shaped tree:

```text
estimate_tree
  root: PageRank under 10GB cap
  operator: max_of_phases

  phase: projection/build
    operator: sum
    components: id-map, adjacency, weights, properties

  phase: algorithm/run
    operator: sum_or_streaming_max
    components: rank-vector, delta-vector, degree-cache, message-slab

  phase: output/writeback
    operator: max
    components: stream-buffer, write-batch, checksum
```

The product implication is strong. A lower-RAM profile is not credible because
it says "we use less RAM." It is credible when its accounting tree explains
which state is simultaneous, which state is sequential, what numeric min/max
bytes were admitted under the cap, and what measured high-water mark happened
after the run.

Rubber duck check:

```text
If Knight Bus only copies GDS treeView/mapView:
  We get compatibility, but not enough differentiation.

If Knight Bus adds accounting operators and measured phase receipts:
  We can prove why a profile fits in 5GB/10GB without pretending every
  algorithm state is resident at once.

If Knight Bus hides numeric bytes behind human strings:
  LLMs and tests will struggle. Keep display strings, but add machine numeric
  min/max bytes per node.
```

The pass-088 product decision:

```text
Build estimate trees as first-class artifacts.
Each node should have:
  name
  accounting operator
  numeric min/max bytes
  display string
  phase/profile tag
  child nodes
  cap/admission decision
  measured runtime high-water delta
```

#### GDS Guards Turn Estimates Into Admission

Pass 089 adds the next layer above the estimate tree: admission control. GDS
does not only display an estimate. It uses estimates to block or reserve work.

There are two distinct guard points:

| Guard Point | GDS Mechanism | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Projection/build admission | `GraphProjectMemoryUsageService.validateMemoryUsage` -> `MemoryUsageValidator` before `GraphStoreFromDatabaseLoader.graphStore()` | avoids paying graph load/build cost when the estimate cannot fit |
| Algorithm/run admission | `DefaultMemoryGuard.assertAlgorithmCanRun` -> `MemoryRequirement` -> `MemoryTracker.tryToTrack` | avoids starting algorithm work when the task reservation cannot fit |

The important GDS behavior:

```text
Projection path:
  estimate projection memory
  choose min or max estimate by config
  compare to available memory
  if insufficient:
    log exact block reason
    throw IllegalStateException
  if sudo:
    bypass check but still track reservation

Algorithm path:
  compute graph dimensions
  transform dimensions
  estimate algorithm memory with concurrency
  choose min or max required bytes
  reserve bytes with MemoryTracker
  if insufficient:
    throw required-vs-available error
```

For Knight Bus, the wedge is not "we have a guard." GDS already has guards. The
wedge is "our guard can route between physical profiles under an explicit cap."

```text
GDS-like binary guard:
  estimate -> min/max policy -> admit OR block OR sudo

Knight Bus cap router:
  estimate profiles -> sort by RAM/latency tradeoff
  -> admit exact in-RAM profile if it fits
  -> else admit spill/streaming/chunked profile if it fits
  -> else reject with typed reason and suggested cap/runtime tradeoff
  -> after run, attach measured high-water receipt
```

This is the heart of budget-bounded batch compute. The user should be able to
say:

```text
Run WCC under 5GB.
Prefer exact output.
Accept up to 90 minutes.
Fail closed if no exact profile fits.
```

The product should respond with a proof, not a vibe:

```text
selected_profile: wcc_partitioned_union_find_spill_v1
admission: admitted
cap_bytes: 5_000_000_000
estimated_peak_bytes: 4_420_000_000
estimated_runtime: 71 minutes
rejected_profiles:
  - wcc_in_memory_gds_compatible_v1: 18_700_000_000 bytes
  - wcc_bitmap_frontier_v1: 6_300_000_000 bytes
receipt_after_run:
  measured_peak_bytes: ...
  output_checksum: ...
  comparator_delta: ...
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
What GDS already gives us:
  Projection and algorithm memory checks, min/max policy, task reservation,
  failure messages, sudo bypass, and missing-estimate fallback.

What Knight Bus must add:
  Multiple physical profiles, explicit cap, typed rejection reasons, profile
  alternatives, waiver receipts, and measured high-water reconciliation.

What would be weak:
  A smaller byte estimate with no guard, no reservation, no runtime receipt, or
  no explanation of why a slower lower-RAM profile was selected.
```

The pass-089 product decision:

```text
Design cap admission as a first-class router:
  projection/build admission
  algorithm/run admission
  output/writeback admission
  profile alternatives
  sudo/override waiver
  reservation receipt
  high-water reconciliation receipt
```

#### GDS Separates Estimate Policy From Memory Observability

Pass 090 adds two operational details that matter for product shape.

First, the min-vs-max policy is global and defaults to the minimum estimate.
GDS defines `gds.validate_using_max_memory_estimation` with default `false`.
That means the default guard uses the lower bound of an estimate range unless
the setting is enabled.

Second, GDS exposes memory state through procedures:

```text
CALL gds.memory.list
  user
  name
  entity
  memoryInBytes

CALL gds.memory.summary
  user
  totalGraphsMemory
  totalTasksMemory
```

The tests show two important semantics:

```text
Non-admin user:
  sees own graph/task memory only

Admin user:
  sees all graph/task memory
```

This splits the product surface into three modes:

| Mode | GDS Shape | Knight Bus Shape |
|---|---|---|
| Estimate-only | `.estimate` returns a result row; no reservation is made | produce estimate tree and profile alternatives, explicitly mark no reservation |
| Admission | projection/algorithm guard validates and reserves | route among profiles under cap, reserve selected profile, record rejected profiles |
| Observability | `gds.memory.list/summary` show graph/task reservations | show reservation, cap, profile, high-water, spill bytes, release status, and estimate error |

This is a subtle but decisive product distinction. If a user runs `.estimate`,
they should know it is a prediction artifact. If a user runs the job, they
should get an admission artifact and a reservation artifact. If the job is
running, they should be able to query the live ledger.

Rubber duck check:

```text
What GDS already gives:
  A global min/max validation setting, memory list, memory summary, graph-size
  fields, user/admin isolation, and task/graph reservation rows.

What Knight Bus should improve:
  Per-job cap policy instead of only global policy, live profile visibility,
  measured high-water bytes, spill bytes, release timestamps, and estimate
  error after completion.

What would confuse users:
  Letting estimate-only rows look like admitted jobs, or letting admitted jobs
  disappear without a live reservation and completion receipt.
```

The pass-090 product decision:

```text
Make memory policy and observability first-class:
  estimate_only_receipt
  admission_receipt
  reservation_ledger_row
  running_job_memory_row
  completed_job_reconciliation_row
```

#### GDS Graph-Size Details Show What A Cap Ledger Must Explain

Pass 091 makes the previous memory-observability point sharper.

The reservation ledger says "how much memory is reserved". The graph-size
detail map says "where the projected graph memory actually sits". GDS already
has the raw vocabulary:

```text
detailSizeInBytes
  total
  nodes
    sparseLongArray
    forwardMapping
    backwardMapping
    mapping
    total
  relationships
    degrees
    offsets
    targetIds
    adjacencyLists
    total
  adjacencyLists
    <relationshipType>
      pages
      bytesTotal
      bytesOnHeap
      bytesOffHeap
      pageSizes
      heapAllocations
      nativeAllocations
      headerAllocations
      headerBits
      optional packed block and bit-width statistics
```

That shape is exactly what Knight Bus needs, except profile-aware and
cap-aware. A lower-RAM claim is weak if it only says:

```text
Neo4j: 50 GB
Knight Bus: 12 GB
```

The stronger product receipt says:

```text
Why the selected profile fits:
  node mapping bytes reduced by dense ID reuse
  degree/offset arrays kept resident
  target IDs stored as profile-specific compressed pages
  packed/native pages bounded separately from heap
  frontier/work buffers capped by phase
  spill or mmap bytes disclosed separately
  measured high-water reconciled after completion
```

This also separates three different ledgers that should not be confused:

| Ledger | Question Answered | GDS Clue | Knight Bus Upgrade |
|---|---|---|---|
| Estimate tree | What should this job need before it starts? | `.estimate`, memory tree, min/max policy | profile alternatives, cap policy, predicted phase high-water |
| Reservation ledger | What did we admit and reserve? | `gds.memory.list`, task/graph reservations | profile, cap, spill budget, live status, release timestamp |
| Actual graph-size map | What is currently resident and where? | `gds.internal.graph.sizeOf`, `detailSizeInBytes` | per-storage-format component map before/after run |

The mixed compression code is especially useful as a mental model. It merges
vlong on-heap pages/degrees/offsets with packed off-heap and header statistics.
That is a tiny version of the product architecture we want: choose a physical
shape, keep the bookkeeping separated, and expose enough detail for a user to
audit why the job fit.

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we emit only total bytes:
  users cannot tell whether the saving is real, accidental, or shifted into
  native/mmap/spill space.

If we emit component bytes without cap/admission state:
  we have diagnostics, not a budget-bounded product.

If we emit estimate tree + admission + reservation + component graph-size map:
  the lower-RAM claim becomes inspectable, falsifiable, and useful for reruns.
```

The pass-091 product decision:

```text
Every storage profile should produce a graph_size_detail_map before and after
run, plus a high-water reconciliation row. PageRank, WCC, BFS, similarity, and
complex-read profiles can use different storage formats, but each must report
the same component ledger vocabulary.
```

#### GDS Estimate Fixtures Show The Verification Loop Starts Before Hot Loops

Pass 092 adds the estimate-fixture layer underneath the cap ledger.

The mistake would be to begin by rewriting PageRank or WCC and only later ask
whether the memory math is correct. GDS shows the opposite order. The estimate
surface is already executable:

```text
CALL gds.wcc.stream.estimate(...)
  -> exactly one row
  -> requiredMemory
  -> treeView
  -> mapView
  -> bytesMin
  -> bytesMax
  -> nodeCount
  -> relationshipCount
  -> heapPercentageMin
  -> heapPercentageMax
```

The tests exercise multiple input modes:

| Input Mode | GDS Fixture Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Named projected graph | `gds.wcc.stream.estimate('graph', {})` after `gds.graph.project` | dimensions come from a real catalog graph; estimate is algorithm-only in the central executor path |
| Fictitious graph map | `{nodeCount, relationshipCount, nodeProjection, relationshipProjection}` | dimensions are user-supplied; useful for planning before data exists |
| Native projection map | `{nodeProjection, relationshipProjection}` | dimensions come from database projection planning |
| Graph project estimate | `gds.graph.project.estimate(...)` | projection/loading memory can be tested independently from algorithm memory |

The important engineering clue is that some fixture bytes are exact. GDS pins
projection estimates for tiny and enormous virtual graphs, including a
5-billion-node and 20-billion-relationship fixture. That is not a marketing
benchmark; it is arithmetic discipline.

For Knight Bus, this becomes a sequencing rule:

```text
1. Implement estimate schema fixtures first.
2. Implement exact byte fixtures for toy graphs and large virtual graphs.
3. Implement cap/admission behavior against those estimates.
4. Implement graph-size detail maps and high-water reconciliation.
5. Only then optimize algorithm hot loops and storage profiles.
```

The disabled Cypher projection property fixture is also useful. It says a
professional estimate surface can carry unsupported or unsettled areas without
pretending parity is complete. Knight Bus should explicitly mark unsupported
projection/property/profile combinations in receipts.

Rubber duck check:

```text
If estimates are only docs:
  LLMs will drift; future storage profiles will invent byte math.

If estimates are executable fixtures:
  storage work has a contract before code exists.

If estimates distinguish named, native, fictitious, and projection-loading paths:
  users can understand the evidence tier of a claim.
```

The pass-092 product decision:

```text
Build the first proof-carrying slice around estimate fixtures before algorithm
speed. A credible lower-RAM graph product should be able to answer: what input
mode was estimated, which bytes were graph-loading bytes, which bytes were
algorithm bytes, what cap was applied, and which parts are unsupported.
```

#### GDS Algorithm Estimates Are Byte Algebra, Not Comments

Pass 093 moves one layer deeper: from estimate rows and execution paths into
the algorithm byte formulas themselves.

The useful discovery is that the algorithms are not one category. They fall
into different memory-contract families:

| Algorithm | GDS Estimate Shape | What It Implies For Knight Bus |
|---|---|---|
| WCC | One disjoint-set component, non-incremental or incremental | A concurrency-invariant per-node state profile with a very clear lower-RAM target: make connected-component state smaller, streamed, or segmented without breaking union/find semantics |
| PageRank | Pregel envelope with vote bits, compute steps, node value, and message arrays | A generic iterative-message profile where storage and memory claims must separate graph storage, rank vectors, vote bits, and send/receive buffers |
| BFS | Per-node resident state plus a `localNodes` min/max range affected by relationships and concurrency | A frontier-sensitive profile where bounded-RAM mode can intentionally trade time for smaller frontier batches |

This is the right abstraction level for a rewrite. Do not start by saying:

```text
Rewrite PageRank in Rust.
```

Start by saying:

```text
Port the PageRank estimate tree, fixtures, and receipt first.
Then implement one runtime profile that must explain each measured byte
against the estimate tree.
```

The WCC numbers are especially grounding:

```text
Non-incremental WCC:
  0 nodes              -> 64 bytes
  100 nodes            -> 864 bytes
  100,000,000,000 nodes -> 800,122,070,392 bytes

Incremental WCC:
  0 nodes              -> 104 bytes
  100 nodes            -> 1,704 bytes
  100,000,000,000 nodes -> 1,600,244,140,760 bytes

Concurrency invariant at 100 nodes:
  non-incremental: 1, 4, 128 threads -> 864 bytes
  incremental:     1, 4, 128 threads -> 1,704 bytes
```

That tells us the exact product wording: WCC is not where concurrency should
surprise users in the memory estimate. If Knight Bus offers WCC profiles, the
receipt should say whether the selected profile is:

```text
dense_parent_array
segmented_parent_array
compressed_parent_delta_pages
disk_backed_union_log_plus_checkpoint
approx_or_sampled_component_profile
```

and the estimate should stay explainable through the same component language.

PageRank is different. The estimate is a Pregel envelope:

```text
Pregel
  vote bits
  compute steps per thread
  node value
    PAGE_RANK (DOUBLE)
  message arrays
    send array
    receive array
```

The PageRank fixture grows slightly with concurrency at 100k nodes and 1M
relationships:

```text
concurrency 1  -> 2,412,832 bytes
concurrency 4  -> 2,413,000 bytes
concurrency 42 -> 2,415,128 bytes
```

The important lesson is not that those exact JVM bytes are our target. The
lesson is that the concurrency delta has a named source: per-thread compute
steps. Knight Bus receipts should make small concurrency overheads explicit so
users know whether a cap failure came from rank vectors, message buffers,
thread-local state, graph storage, or frontier materialization.

BFS is the clearest RAM/latency tradeoff example. GDS models `localNodes` as a
range:

```text
lowerBound = sizeOfLongArrayList(nodeCount + nodeCount / 64)
upperBound = sizeOfLongArrayList(
  min(relCountUpperBound, concurrency * (nodeCount - 1)) + nodeCount / 64
)
```

The fixtures show the range widening when concurrency rises:

```text
10k nodes / 100k rels / concurrency 1 -> 402,988 .. 402,988
10k nodes / 100k rels / concurrency 2 -> 402,988 .. 482,972

100k nodes / 1M rels / concurrency 1 -> 4,026,890 .. 4,026,890
100k nodes / 1M rels / concurrency 2 -> 4,026,890 .. 4,826,874
```

This is exactly where Knight Bus can differentiate. A bounded profile can say:

```text
I will cap local frontier memory.
I may run more phases or perform more sequential frontier draining.
I will report the chosen cap, frontier spill/mmap bytes, phase count, and
measured high-water bytes.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If fixture bytes exist without formula traces:
  the tests catch drift but humans and LLMs cannot explain why the bytes moved.

If formula traces exist without golden fixtures:
  the design sounds nice but no one can tell when arithmetic breaks.

If formula traces, component trees, golden fixtures, and high-water receipts
all exist:
  the rewrite has a verification spine before storage innovation begins.
```

The pass-093 product decision:

```text
The first implementation milestone should port estimate algebra and golden
fixtures for WCC, PageRank, and BFS before optimizing runtime storage. Those
three algorithms give us the three families we need: concurrency-invariant
per-node state, iterative Pregel-style state, and frontier-sensitive ranges.
```

#### Runtime Ownership Shows Where Storage Innovation Should Attach

Pass 094 asks a sharper question: do the estimate trees map to real runtime
objects, or are they only accounting descriptions?

For the three inspected algorithms, the answer is mostly yes:

| Algorithm | Estimate Component | Runtime Owner | Knight Bus Attack Point |
|---|---|---|---|
| WCC | DSS `data` | `HugeAtomicDisjointSetStruct.parent` | parent array layout, segmented union state, compressed checkpoint plus union log |
| WCC seeded/incremental | DSS `seeding information` | `HugeAtomicDisjointSetStruct.communities` plus `maxCommunityId` | optional seeded profile, explicit seed-state receipt |
| PageRank | node value DOUBLE | `NodeValue.of` / `HugeDoubleArray` | rank-vector layout, mmap vector, compressed delta vector, phase-local vector |
| PageRank | message arrays | `ReducingMessenger.sendArray` / `receiveArray` | double-buffer policy, sparse active-message profile, chunked message pages |
| PageRank | vote bits | `HugeAtomicBitSet` | bitset compression is probably not the first win, but it should stay visible |
| BFS | `visited`, `traversedNodes`, `weights`, `minimumChunk` | resident graph-sized arrays in `BFS.create` / `BFS.compute` | fixed resident floor; optimize but do not expect magic here |
| BFS | `localNodes`, `chunks` range | per-task `LongArrayList` buffers in `BFSTask` | bounded frontier capacity, early draining, spill/mmap chunks, lower-concurrency mode |

This changes the implementation strategy.

The weak version of the rewrite says:

```text
Use Rust and io_uring and hope hot loops are faster.
```

The stronger version says:

```text
For each algorithm family, identify the runtime state owner.
Attach a storage profile to that owner.
Emit an estimate tree before execution and a measured owner-state receipt after execution.
```

WCC is the cleanest starter because the runtime state is mostly one thing:

```text
Wcc.compute
  -> HugeAtomicDisjointSetStruct(parent)
  -> optional HugeAtomicDisjointSetStruct(communities)
  -> sampled or unsampled strategy uses the same DSS
```

That makes WCC good for exactness, not necessarily the most dramatic product
demo. The first WCC profile can prove our machinery: estimate, admission,
runtime receipt, correctness oracle, and high-water reconciliation.

PageRank is the reusable Pregel family:

```text
PageRankAlgorithm
  -> Pregel.create
    -> NodeValue.of(schema)
      -> HugeDoubleArray for PAGE_RANK
    -> HugeAtomicBitSet vote bits
    -> ReducingMessenger send/receive arrays
    -> PartitionedComputer / PartitionedComputeStep references
```

The likely storage innovation is not "make PageRank one array smaller." It is
making iterative state explicit and selectable:

```text
dense_in_ram_vectors
mmap_rank_vectors
sparse_active_message_vectors
chunked_double_buffered_messages
phase_local_delta_vectors
```

BFS is the most product-visible bounded-RAM wedge:

```text
BFS resident floor:
  visited
  traversedNodes
  weights
  minimumChunk

BFS variable frontier:
  one localNodes LongArrayList per task
  one chunks LongArrayList per task
  synchronization from local buffers into global traversedNodes
```

That means a bounded profile can be honest:

```text
I cannot remove all resident graph-sized state without a deeper algorithm
change, but I can cap local frontier materialization and disclose the time cost.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If the estimate tree has no runtime owner:
  the receipt cannot explain measured memory.

If the runtime owner has no estimate component:
  the estimate is incomplete or the runtime object is too small to matter.

If owner, estimate, fixture, and receipt line up:
  LLM-coded Rust can port the state family one owner at a time.
```

The pass-094 product decision:

```text
Make "runtime state owner" a first-class receipt dimension. The first prototype
should not only say WCC/PageRank/BFS used X bytes; it should say which owner
held those bytes, which profile controlled it, and whether the measured owner
state matched the estimate component.
```

#### Correctness Oracles Define The Minimum Proof-Carrying Slice

Pass 095 adds the missing third leg. Estimate arithmetic tells us what should
fit. Runtime ownership tells us where the bytes actually live. Correctness
oracles tell us whether an algorithm-shaped storage change still computes the
same thing.

The minimum proof-carrying slice now looks like this:

```text
1. estimate fixture
   -> exact component tree and expected min/max bytes

2. runtime owner receipt
   -> which object/profile actually held each large state component

3. correctness oracle
   -> same result semantics as Neo4j/GDS for the fixture

4. cap/admission receipt
   -> selected RAM cap, selected profile, admitted/rejected/fallback status

5. high-water reconciliation
   -> estimated bytes vs measured owner bytes vs measured process/job high-water
```

For WCC, the oracle is partition-shaped:

```text
Do all nodes that should belong together resolve to the same component?
Do nodes in different expected regions stay in different components?
Does seeded/incremental mode merge communities deterministically?
Does minComponentSize filtering preserve pairwise component equivalence?
```

This is ideal for a first exactness proof because the internal component id can
vary while the user-visible partition remains the same. That gives Knight Bus
freedom to use segmented parent arrays, compressed parent checkpoints, or a
union-log profile without forcing byte-for-byte internal id parity.

For PageRank, the oracle is numeric and procedural:

```text
Do node scores match expected values within epsilon?
Does tolerance change convergence iteration count as expected?
Do weighted and unweighted variants match expected scores?
Do stream/stats/mutate modes report the right fields, convergence state,
iteration count, written property count, and mutated graph?
```

This is stricter. A storage profile that changes floating-point accumulation
order may still be acceptable, but only if the tolerance oracle explicitly says
so. If we want an approximate PageRank mode later, it should be named as
approximate and should have separate quality/error receipts.

For BFS, the oracle is frontier-behavior-shaped:

```text
Does target breaking return the expected mapped-node order?
Does incoming direction traverse the reverse graph correctly?
Does max depth include exactly the allowed layers?
Does a loop graph terminate?
Do multi-target and larger-frontier fixtures preserve layer/order behavior
under concurrency and delta variants?
```

This is the direct proof surface for bounded-RAM BFS. If we cap local frontier
buffers, drain chunks earlier, spill chunks, or lower concurrency, the output
must still satisfy the target/depth/direction/loop/order oracles.

The architecture implication is simple:

```text
Do not start with "rewrite Neo4j."
Start with "port one oracle triplet."

For each algorithm:
  estimate fixture
  runtime owner receipt
  correctness oracle
```

The first three triplets should be:

| Algorithm | Estimate Family | Runtime Owner | Correctness Oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| WCC | concurrency-invariant DSS bytes | parent/community DSS arrays | partition equivalence plus seed/min-filter rules |
| PageRank | Pregel node/message/vote arrays | rank vector, send/receive buffers, vote bits | numeric scores, convergence iterations, procedure receipts |
| BFS | frontier-sensitive min/max range | resident arrays plus local chunk buffers | target/depth/direction/loop/order behavior |

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we only prove lower RAM:
  we may have produced a wrong algorithm cheaply.

If we only prove correctness:
  we may have recreated GDS with no differentiation.

If we prove correctness, estimate, owner mapping, cap admission, and high-water:
  we have the unit of product truth for a storage-profile rewrite.
```

The pass-095 product decision:

```text
Make correctness oracles first-class artifacts, not buried tests. Every
lower-RAM profile should name the exact oracle fixture that proves it remained
semantically compatible with Neo4j/GDS.
```

#### API Parity Is A Separate Proof Layer

Pass 096 tightens a mistake that would be easy to make in a Rust rewrite:
algorithm correctness is not the same as Neo4j/GDS surface parity.

For a user, the observable contract is often the procedure row:

```text
gds.wcc.stream
  -> nodeId, componentId

gds.wcc.stats
  -> componentCount, componentDistribution, timings, configuration

gds.wcc.mutate / gds.wcc.write
  -> stats fields + mutateMillis/writeMillis + nodePropertiesWritten

gds.pageRank.stream
  -> nodeId, score

gds.pageRank.stats / mutate / write
  -> ranIterations, didConverge, centralityDistribution, timings,
     configuration, and side-effect fields

gds.bfs.stream
  -> sourceNode, nodeIds, path
```

That is a different proof surface from the algorithm's internal state.

The full proof stack is now:

```text
Estimate proof:
  Does the component formula predict memory?

Runtime-owner proof:
  Did the predicted state appear at the expected owner?

Correctness proof:
  Did the algorithm return the right semantic answer?

API-parity proof:
  Did the procedure return the right columns, ids, timings, side effects,
  distributions, path objects, configuration echoes, and validation errors?

Budget proof:
  Did the run stay inside the declared cap/high-water/spill contract?
```

The return-column evidence is especially useful. GDS result builders inspect
`ProcedureReturnColumns`; community count/distribution and centrality
distribution are only computed when requested. That means a lower-latency or
lower-RAM profile cannot treat output schema as passive metadata.

For Knight Bus, `YIELD` should become planner input:

```text
If user requests only nodeId, componentId:
  avoid distribution work.

If user requests componentDistribution:
  schedule histogram post-processing and record its cost.

If user requests PageRank centralityDistribution:
  compute or explain histogram output/error.

If user requests BFS path:
  materialize path object and synthetic NEXT relationships, not just nodeIds.
```

This is also a good Shreyas-style product cut:

```text
The product is not "we rewrote PageRank."
The product is "for this exact GDS call shape, we can tell you before running:
which profile will execute, how much RAM it will use, what latency tradeoff it
implies, which output columns will trigger extra work, and which fixture proves
the result remains compatible."
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If the algorithm is correct but the row schema is wrong:
  users cannot swap it into Neo4j/GDS-style workflows.

If the row schema is right but optional post-processing is always executed:
  latency predictability gets worse and the budget story becomes less honest.

If requested columns drive planning and receipts:
  surface-area compatibility becomes a lever for lower cost, not only a burden.
```

The pass-096 product decision:

```text
Make API parity receipts a first-class test family beside algorithm oracles.
The first prototype should prove one stream/stats/mutate/write surface where
available, and should record requested columns as part of the execution plan.
```

#### Profile Selection Belongs Between Parsed Request And Algorithm Run

Pass 097 answers a practical architecture question:

```text
If we keep the Neo4j/GDS surface area, where does a custom storage profile
actually plug in?
```

The answer from GDS source is: not in the public procedure wrapper.

The public wrapper/facade path is mostly a compatibility shell:

```text
Public procedure
  -> local procedure facade
  -> parse mode-specific config
  -> inspect requested return columns
  -> bind mode-specific result builder
  -> call algorithm-family business facade
  -> call algorithm processing template
  -> load graph resources
  -> memory guard / admission
  -> compute algorithm
  -> side effects for mutate/write
  -> render result rows
```

For Knight Bus, the storage-profile selector should sit in the reusable
execution envelope, not inside every procedure:

```text
parsed config + graph resources + algorithm label + mode + requested columns
  -> candidate storage profiles
  -> estimate each profile
  -> reject profiles that violate RAM/deadline/exactness
  -> select profile
  -> bind graph view/state layout for compute
  -> run algorithm
  -> render same API surface
  -> emit receipt
```

This matters because WCC, PageRank, and BFS all converge into a similar
shape:

```text
WCC:
  LocalCommunityProcedureFacade.wccStream
    -> CommunityAlgorithmsStreamModeBusinessFacade.wcc
    -> processRegularAlgorithmInStreamMode(WCC, estimate, algorithms.wcc, resultBuilder)

PageRank:
  LocalCentralityProcedureFacade.pageRankStream
    -> CentralityAlgorithmsStreamModeBusinessFacade.pageRank
    -> processRegularAlgorithmInStreamMode(PageRank, estimate, centralityAlgorithms.pageRank, resultBuilder)

BFS:
  LocalPathFindingProcedureFacade.breadthFirstSearchStream
    -> PathFindingAlgorithmsStreamModeBusinessFacade.breadthFirstSearch
    -> processRegularAlgorithmInStreamMode(BFS, estimate, algorithms.breadthFirstSearch, resultBuilder)
```

Then the default processing template does the operational work:

```text
loadAndValidateGraph
  -> graphStoreCatalogService.getGraphResources(...)

runComputation
  -> computationService.computeAlgorithm(...)

computeAlgorithm
  -> memoryGuard.assertAlgorithmCanRun(...)
  -> computeWithMetrics(...)

computeWithMetrics
  -> computation.compute(graphResources.graph(), graphResources.graphStore())

render
  -> resultRenderer.render(...)
```

The most interesting source detail is that GDS already has a decorator seam:
`LocalGraphDataScienceProcedures.createAlgorithmProcessingTemplate` accepts an
`algorithmProcessingTemplateDecorator`. That is not proof that Neo4j intends
third-party storage-profile injection there, but it is evidence that the
template boundary is an intentional cross-cutting boundary.

Knight Bus should copy the shape, not necessarily the Java class names:

```text
ProfileAwareAlgorithmTemplate
  wraps:
    load graph resources
    estimate/admit
    compute
    side effect
    render

  adds:
    candidate profile enumeration
    per-profile memory/latency estimate
    profile selection
    fallback rejection reasons
    profile-specific graph view/state binding
    proof-carrying receipt
```

The pass-097 product decision:

```text
Do not fork the public procedure surface first.
First build a uniform execution-template receipt:
procedure -> facade -> config -> graph resources -> estimate -> memory guard
-> selected profile -> algorithm compute -> result builder -> output rows.

Then implement custom WCC/PageRank/BFS storage profiles underneath that
receipt boundary.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If profile selection happens too high:
  every procedure becomes bespoke and API parity becomes fragile.

If profile selection happens too low:
  the planner cannot see requested columns, mode, config, user/job, or
  side-effect requirements.

If profile selection happens at the execution-template boundary:
  one planner can reason across WCC, PageRank, BFS, and future algorithms while
  still preserving each algorithm's result-builder contract.
```

#### Profile Alternatives Need Admission Receipts

Pass 098 turns the pass-097 hook point into a more concrete planner shape.

GDS already has the skeleton of a serious production guard:

```text
algorithm label + graph store + algorithm config + dimension transformer
  -> graph dimensions
  -> transformed dimensions
  -> memory estimation tree
  -> memory range
  -> min/max policy
  -> required bytes
  -> available memory check
  -> task reservation or failure
```

But it is intentionally binary:

```text
one algorithm/config path
  -> one selected memory requirement
  -> pass, fail, skip-estimate, or sudo
```

Knight Bus should generalize this into a router:

```text
graph dimensions + config + requested columns + user cap + deadline/exactness
  -> profile candidates
  -> profile-specific dimension transforms
  -> profile-specific component estimate trees
  -> min/max/percentile admission policy
  -> live graph/task memory context
  -> accept/reject all candidates
  -> select the best admissible profile
  -> reserve by job id
  -> run
  -> release
  -> reconcile estimated vs measured high-water bytes
```

That matters because lower RAM is not one architecture.

For WCC, a profile might change the disjoint-set parent/community layout:
full resident atomic longs, segmented mmap pages, compressed component labels,
checkpointed parent pages, or partition-local merge logs.

For PageRank, a profile might change vector and message layout:
full resident double vectors, mmap-backed value vectors, sparse active-delta
vectors, chunked rank windows, compressed send/receive buffers, or convergence
phases that trade wall time for bounded resident state.

For BFS, a profile might change frontier/result materialization:
full resident visited/traversed arrays, bitmap frontier, chunked frontier,
spill-backed frontier, endpoint-only output, path-on-demand output, or lowered
concurrency under a strict cap.

The key product move is to show all of that before running:

```text
candidate: bfs_full_resident
  required: 94 GB
  status: rejected
  reason: exceeds 10 GB cap

candidate: bfs_chunked_frontier
  required: 8.7 GB
  status: admitted
  expected latency: higher
  exactness: exact

candidate: bfs_spill_frontier
  required: 4.2 GB resident + spill
  status: admitted
  expected latency: much higher
  exactness: exact
```

That is the point where the rewrite becomes meaningfully different from
"Neo4j/GDS but in Rust." GDS's guard is good safety infrastructure; Knight Bus
should make it product-shaped by turning admission into an inspectable choice
among lower-RAM algorithm-specific storage plans.

The pass-098 product decision:

```text
Do not build a single memory guard. Build a profile-admission engine.
Every run should produce an admission receipt that lists accepted and rejected
profiles, free/reserved/cap bytes, min/max policy, override status, reservation
release, and post-run estimate error.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If the planner only records the selected profile:
  future users cannot see what tradeoffs were rejected or why the cap mattered.

If the planner records alternatives but does not reserve memory:
  the estimate is not an operational guarantee; another task can consume memory
  between planning and execution.

If the planner reserves memory but does not reconcile after the run:
  the system never learns whether its estimates are conservative, optimistic,
  or profile-specific nonsense.

If the planner records alternatives, reserves by job id, releases, and
reconciles high-water:
  the product can make bounded-RAM claims that are inspectable and improvable.
```

#### Side Effects Are A Separate Budget Phase

Pass 099 sharpens the profile-admission engine: the selected profile must fit
not only the algorithm's working set but also the requested output mode.

GDS makes this visible in its shared template:

```text
load and validate graph
  -> run computation
  -> process optional side effect
  -> render result row
```

The side-effect stage is optional, timed separately, and mode-specific. If the
algorithm returns no result, `SideEffectExecutor` skips the side effect. If a
mutate or write side effect exists, the shared template records side-effect
millis and passes side-effect metadata to the mode-specific result builder.

That means the lower-RAM planner should not ask only:

```text
Can PageRank/WCC/BFS compute under the RAM cap?
```

It must ask:

```text
Can this exact mode finish under the RAM cap?

mode = stream
  compute output rows only

mode = stats
  compute summaries/distributions if requested

mode = mutate
  compute algorithm result
  materialize node-property values
  add resident state to the in-memory graph store

mode = write
  compute algorithm result
  materialize node-property values
  resolve result-store behavior
  build exporter
  write with configured concurrency
  release progress tracker
```

WCC and PageRank prove the difference.

WCC write mode computes the disjoint-set result, transforms it into community
node-property values through `CommunityCompanion.nodePropertyValues`, writes
those values through `WriteToDatabase.perform`, and returns both
`NodePropertiesWritten` and the values. WCC mutate mode performs a similar
component-value transformation but commits the values into the graph store.

PageRank is simpler but still modeful: write mode sends
`result.nodePropertyValues()` through the database writer, while mutate mode
adds those node-property values to the graph store.

The practical consequence:

```text
profile compute fit
  does not imply
profile mutate/write fit
```

A candidate profile can be perfectly admissible for `gds.pageRank.stream`, then
fail for `gds.pageRank.mutate` because the output vector must become resident
graph-store property state. Another profile can fit `wcc.stats` but fail
`wcc.write` because component values and exporter buffers exceed the cap at the
writeback phase.

So the Knight Bus receipt should split the run into phase budgets:

```text
projection/build bytes
algorithm working bytes
post-processing bytes
mutate graph-store residency bytes
write/exporter bytes
result-store bytes
release/reconciliation state
```

That gives the user a much more honest product experience:

```text
candidate: pagerank_full_resident_stream
  compute: admitted
  side_effect: none
  total cap: admitted

candidate: pagerank_chunked_vector_mutate
  compute: admitted
  mutate output residency: rejected
  reason: score property would exceed remaining graph-store cap

candidate: pagerank_spill_vector_write
  compute: admitted
  write exporter: admitted
  result store: disabled
  expected latency: higher
  exactness: exact
```

The design rule from this pass:

```text
Treat stream, stats, mutate, and write as separate memory contracts.
The public API surface can stay Neo4j/GDS-like, but the planner must choose and
prove a profile for the entire mode, not only the hot algorithm loop.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If the planner ignores side effects:
  it can promise a 10GB PageRank and then exceed the cap while mutating or
  writing results.

If mutate/output bytes are counted but not separated:
  users cannot understand whether the algorithm was expensive or the requested
  output mode was expensive.

If side-effect caps are admitted before execution and reconciled after:
  the product can offer bounded compute modes like "exact, slower, write under
  5GB" with a concrete receipt.
```

#### Writeback Has Two Storage Shapes

Pass 100 makes the side-effect phase sharper: `write` is not one thing.

In the local GDS source, node-property writeback can be viewed as two different
storage shapes behind a shared builder surface:

```text
NodePropertyExporterBuilder
  carries:
    node count
    node labels
    internal -> original id mapping
    termination flag
    write concurrency
    progress tracker
    optional result store
    job id

  native provider
    -> NativeNodePropertyExporter

  result-store provider
    -> ResultStoreNodePropertyExporter
```

The native shape is a database mutation loop:

```text
resolve property token
convert NodePropertyValues to Neo4j values
begin progress subtask
for each internal node id:
  check termination
  compute property value
  skip null values
  map to original node id
  write node property through Neo4j Write API
  increment propertiesWritten
end progress subtask
```

Parallel native mode adds batch sizing, lazy runnable creation, concurrency,
wait/retry behavior, and termination behavior. The integration tests reload the
graph and compare expected GDL after one-property and multi-property writes.
They also prove progress logging and cancellation behavior: when termination is
already false, the write fails and no `foo` property is left behind.

The result-store shape is a deferred artifact:

```text
collect property keys
collect NodePropertyValues references
sum nodeCount across values into propertiesWritten
store ResultStoreEntry.NodeProperties(jobId, labels, keys, values, toOriginalId)
```

The result store is documented as holding write results that are not immediately
persisted, especially for session-style workflows that stream results later to a
remote database. The concrete `EphemeralResultStore` is a job-id keyed Caffeine
cache with a ten-minute expire-after-access policy; `EmptyResultStore` is a
disabled no-op/null implementation.

The budget consequence is subtle:

```text
native writeback:
  more immediate I/O and transaction work
  less long-lived result artifact inside GDS
  proof target is persisted graph equality

result-store writeback:
  less immediate database mutation
  more resident/deferred artifact state
  proof target is entry shape plus later materialization
```

That is directly useful for Knight Bus.

We can make result artifacts a product feature, but only if we avoid the trap of
calling them "free." A deferred result store can save latency to the database or
enable remote/session architecture, but if it retains rank vectors, community
vectors, relationship streams, and id mappings in RAM, it is still consuming the
same kind of scarce budget the user wanted bounded.

The stronger Knight Bus design is:

```text
write target candidates:
  native_database_write
  in_memory_result_store
  mmap_result_store
  sqlite_result_store
  object_store_result_bundle
  disabled_writeback_stream_only

for each target:
  estimate resident bytes
  estimate mapped bytes
  estimate write/export latency
  estimate cleanup/retention cost
  choose against RAM cap and deadline
  emit lifecycle receipt
```

This also gives a clean differentiation path:

```text
Neo4j/GDS compatibility:
  preserve write/mutate result rows and graph-store/database semantics.

Knight Bus differentiation:
  offer lower-RAM result-store profiles with explicit artifact lifetimes,
  filesystem/SQLite/mmap storage, resumable materialization, and exact parity
  fixtures.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we only budget algorithm state:
  writeback can blow the cap after the "successful" run.

If we store deferred results only in RAM:
  we have moved the memory problem, not solved it.

If we make result artifacts external, typed, and lifecycle-managed:
  users can choose slower writeback or later materialization while keeping a
  hard resident-RAM promise.
```

#### Relationship Writeback Has Four Artifact Families

Pass 101 extends the writeback thesis from node properties to relationships.
This matters because many of the most commercially interesting OLAP outputs are
not just node scores. Link prediction, KNN, similarity, path finding, graph
catalog exports, and relationship-property projections can all create or expose
relationship-shaped results.

The local GDS source makes the split concrete:

```text
relationship writeback
  topology-only graph write
    RelationshipExporter

  graph write with one property
    RelationshipExporter

  stream of exported relationships
    RelationshipStreamExporter

  graph-store relationship properties
    RelationshipPropertiesExporter
```

In native database writeback, these become mutation loops:

```text
NativeRelationshipExporter
  degree partition graph
  copy relationship iterator per task
  create relationships through Neo4j Write API
  optionally set one translated property
  log progress
  check termination

NativeRelationshipStreamExporter
  force incoming stream to sequential
  allocate two write buffers and two pool buffers
  fill buffers from ExportedRelationship stream
  hand buffers to background writer
  flush final non-full buffer
  write empty sentinel
  return writer.written

NativeRelationshipPropertiesExporter
  get graph by relationship type
  get composite relationship iterator
  create relationships
  write multiple translated properties
  log progress
```

In result-store mode, the artifacts are not one shape:

```text
ResultStoreEntry.RelationshipTopology
  relationship type
  graph reference
  original-id mapping

ResultStoreEntry.RelationshipsFromGraph
  relationship type
  one property key
  graph reference
  original-id mapping

ResultStoreEntry.RelationshipStream
  relationship type
  property keys
  property value types
  stream of ExportedRelationship
  original-id mapping

ResultStoreEntry.RelationshipIterators
  relationship type
  property keys
  composite relationship iterator
  original-id mapping
  node count
```

The product consequence is big:

```text
Node-property output:
  mostly vector-shaped.

Relationship output:
  topology-shaped, stream-shaped, iterator-shaped, and property-matrix-shaped.

Therefore:
  "write result to lower-RAM storage" needs a separate profile family for each
  relationship output shape.
```

For Knight Bus, the useful architecture is not just "use SQLite" or "use mmap."
It is:

```text
if output is topology-only:
  externalize as typed edge bundle:
    src_ids
    dst_ids
    relationship_type
    id-map manifest
    optional sort order

if output is one scalar property:
  externalize as typed edge bundle plus one value column:
    src_ids
    dst_ids
    property_values
    missing/NaN policy

if output is many properties:
  externalize as edge bundle plus column family:
    src_ids
    dst_ids
    property column directory
    value type manifest
    per-column compression stats

if output is a stream:
  either materialize under cap before store
  or mark as one-shot stream with strict consumer lifecycle
```

This points to a stronger v1 contract than GDS exposes in the inspected OSS
path:

```text
relationship_output_profile_v1:
  input source:
    graph | relationship stream | graph-store iterator

  artifact shape:
    topology | one_property | many_properties | stream

  residency:
    resident bytes
    mapped bytes
    spill bytes
    iterator/stream lifetime

  parity:
    result-store entry shape
    native persisted graph equality
    scalar/array property value proof
    duplicate-edge policy
    empty-stream behavior
    buffer-flush behavior
    permission/cancellation behavior
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we only optimize algorithm state:
  a link-prediction write can still allocate buffers, streams, iterators, or
  database mutations that violate the user's RAM cap.

If we store relationship streams lazily without a lifecycle contract:
  we may have reduced immediate database latency while creating a fragile
  one-shot object that is hard to account for.

If we externalize edge/result bundles with typed manifests:
  we can give the user a bounded resident-memory promise and still support
  later materialization into Neo4j-compatible write modes.
```

#### Algorithm Families Choose Different Relationship Output Carriers

Pass 102 turns the relationship-writeback spine into algorithm-specific output
evidence. The main lesson is subtle but important:

```text
The algorithm family name is not enough to choose storage.
The output carrier chooses storage.
```

GDS path-finding alone has several carriers:

```text
Bellman-Ford / shortest path variants
  PathResult stream
    -> ExportedRelationship
      -> totalCost
      -> optional nodeIds array
      -> optional costs array
    -> RelationshipStreamExporter

Spanning tree / Steiner tree
  SpanningTree result
    -> SpanningGraph wrapper
    -> RelationshipExporter
    -> expected written count = effectiveNodeCount - 1

K-spanning tree
  SpanningTreeBackedNodePropertyValues
    -> NodePropertyExporter
    -> not relationship output despite living in the path-finding write family
```

Similarity has a cleaner shape:

```text
KNN / filtered KNN
  SimilarityResult stream
    -> SimilarityGraphResult
    -> similarity graph
    -> RelationshipExporter with score consumer

Node similarity / filtered node similarity
  prebuilt SimilarityGraphResult
    -> similarity graph
    -> RelationshipExporter with score consumer
```

KGE and link-prediction pipelines share the exporter spine, but they introduce
model/pipeline/top-k artifacts:

```text
Link prediction pipeline
  relationshipExporterBuilder travels inside ExecutionContext
  actual output shape is resolved deeper in the pipeline executor

KGE predict write
  topKMap -> TopKGraph -> RelationshipExporter
```

The architecture implication:

```text
profile selection key =
  algorithm
  + mode
  + output carrier
  + output payload shape
  + target materializer
```

This matters for bounded RAM. Shortest-path writeback can look small if we only
count one edge per path, but each edge can carry arrays of path node ids and
costs. Similarity writeback is often a simpler `src, dst, score` bundle.
Spanning-tree writeback is graph-backed and has a predictable edge-count rule.
K-spanning is node-property output and should not be pushed through the
relationship-output lane at all.

One simple carrier-to-storage map:

| Output Carrier | First Storage Format To Try | RAM Control Lever | Verification Hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| Path stream with arrays | chunked path-bundle spool: `src`, `dst`, `total_cost`, varlen `node_ids`, varlen `costs` | cap chunk bytes and spill varlen arrays early | compare path endpoints, total cost, optional node/cost arrays, original-id mapping |
| SpanningGraph relationship output | typed tree-edge bundle: parent/source, child/target, cost/property | edge count bounded by effective nodes | assert `effectiveNodeCount - 1` and graph equality |
| Similarity graph score output | sorted edge-score columns: `src`, `dst`, `score` | top-k/cutoff bounds plus score column compression | assert relationship count, score tolerance, similarity distribution, re-projected graph equality |
| KGE/link-prediction top-k output | candidate-edge score bundle with model provenance sidecar | top-k cap and model artifact cache cap | assert model id, top-k map, relationship count, and output graph |
| K-spanning node property | node-property vector bundle | vector bytes and graph-store residency | assert node-property values, property name, graph-store/result-store parity |

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we say "custom relationship storage" as one feature:
  we will miss path-array payloads, top-k candidate state, and graph-backed
  tree outputs.

If we choose the storage format from the output carrier:
  each algorithm can have a smaller, more predictable artifact with a direct
  parity oracle.

If we build the first proof slice around similarity edge scores:
  the output shape is simpler than path arrays and more product-visible than
  node-property vectors.
```

New executable-spec candidates:

| Candidate | Contract |
|---|---|
| `profile_pathfinding_relationship_stream_receipt_v1` | WHEN a path-finding write emits relationship rows, THEN path source, target, total cost, optional node-id array, optional cost array, original-id mapping, result-store/native target, and payload bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_result_store_eager_collection_receipt_v1` | WHEN a result-store path would eagerly collect a stream, THEN estimated rows, estimated payload bytes, RAM cap, spill path, and refusal behavior SHALL be recorded before collection. |
| `profile_spanning_graph_relationship_receipt_v1` | WHEN spanning or Steiner tree writes relationships, THEN graph wrapper, property key, expected edge-count rule, result-store/native target, and parity oracle SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_edge_score_bundle_receipt_v1` | WHEN KNN or node similarity writes score relationships, THEN source graph shape, root id map, relationship type, score property, distribution policy, count, and score tolerance SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_write_fixture_parity_v1` | WHEN a similarity write fixture runs, THEN one-row write-mode output, timing fields, distribution keys, relationships written, and re-projected graph equality SHALL match the reference. |
| `profile_ml_relationship_output_deferred_receipt_v1` | WHEN ML pipeline outputs are supported, THEN model provenance, pipeline id, candidate graph/top-k map, exporter binding, and relationship count SHALL be part of the receipt. |

#### Starter Slice Output Carriers Are Even Simpler

Pass 103 brings the carrier map back to the first practical rewrite slice:
WCC, PageRank, and BFS. These are not relationship-output algorithms in the
normal starter modes, but they still prove why output carriers matter.

The three starter carriers are:

```text
WCC
  DisjointSetStruct
    -> NodePropertyValues(long componentId)
    -> stream rows: original node id + component id
    -> write/mutate target: node property vector

PageRank
  PageRankResult
    -> NodePropertyValues(double score)
    -> stream rows: original node id + score
    -> write/mutate target: node property vector

BFS
  HugeLongArray traversal result
    -> long[] copy
    -> boxed original-id List<Long>
    -> optional Neo4j Path
    -> one stream row: source node + node list + optional path
```

This is a useful ordering for implementation:

| Order | Slice | Why It Comes Here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | WCC component vector | Integer-valued, deterministic, compact, component-count/distribution fixtures already exist. |
| 2 | PageRank score vector | Same vector carrier, but adds floating tolerance, convergence, iterations, and centrality distribution. |
| 3 | BFS node-list/path materialization | Proves requested output columns change memory usage, because `path` creates extra object materialization. |
| 4 | Similarity edge-score bundle | First relationship-output slice with clean `src,dst,score` shape and graph-equality fixtures. |
| 5 | Path-finding path-array bundles | Harder credibility test because row count hides variable-length path arrays. |

The carrier/target distinction:

```text
carrier:
  the logical output shape the algorithm produced

target:
  where that output goes

same carrier can have multiple targets:
  stream rows
  native database write
  result-store artifact
  graph-store mutation
  external low-RAM bundle
```

For WCC and PageRank, the same `NodePropertyValues` carrier flows to three
different targets:

```text
stream:
  scan internal ids
  filter hasValue
  map to original ids
  emit nodeId + scalar

write:
  validate graph-store write mode
  validate property state
  build node-property exporter
  write native/result-store property
  release progress tracker

mutate:
  optionally wrap values for filtered graph
  add property to graph store
  increase resident graph-store state
```

That target distinction is the real product design point. A user might choose:

```text
stream only:
  lowest durable footprint, but client consumes rows now

result-store artifact:
  avoid immediate database mutation, but lifecycle and materialization must be capped

mutate:
  fastest follow-on graph algorithms, but graph store keeps the new property resident

external profile bundle:
  strongest RAM predictability, but needs explicit materialization/parity commands
```

The BFS lesson is different:

```text
BFS stream result looks like one row.
But that one row can carry an entire traversal node list and optional Path.
```

That means row count is not a sufficient output budget. For traversal outputs,
the receipt needs:

```text
node-list length
node-list bytes before/after id mapping
boxing/list overhead
path requested?
path created?
graph store supports local path creation?
path object length
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we start with PageRank only:
  we prove a famous algorithm but immediately face floating tolerance and
  iterative convergence questions.

If we start with WCC only:
  we prove the cleanest vector carrier, but we might not look exciting.

If we start with WCC + PageRank + BFS as one verification spine:
  we get integer vector, floating vector, and traversal materialization in a
  small enough surface to make receipts real.

If we then add KNN similarity:
  we cross into relationship outputs with a clean edge-score bundle instead of
  jumping straight into path-array complexity.
```

The pass-103 product decision:

```text
The first implementation milestone should not be "rewrite Neo4j."
It should be:

  profile_output_carrier_selector_v1
  + WCC component vector profile
  + PageRank score vector profile
  + BFS node-list/path materialization profile
  + one shared node-property target lifecycle receipt

Only after that should the relationship-output lane start with KNN/similarity.
```

New executable-spec candidates:

| Candidate | Contract |
|---|---|
| `profile_wcc_component_vector_receipt_v1` | WHEN WCC produces stream/write/mutate output, THEN component vector owner, filtering policy, component count, distribution fields, property name, target lifecycle, and node count SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_pagerank_score_vector_receipt_v1` | WHEN PageRank produces stream/write/mutate output, THEN score vector owner, tolerance, convergence flag, iteration count, distribution fields, property name, and target lifecycle SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_bfs_node_list_path_receipt_v1` | WHEN BFS stream output is built, THEN source node, target/depth/direction config, node-list length, original-id mapping, path-requested flag, path-created status, and materialization bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_node_property_target_lifecycle_receipt_v1` | WHEN a node-property vector is streamed, written, result-stored, mutated, or externalized, THEN target type, write mode, property state, filtered mapping, result-store/Arrow requirement, progress release, and resident graph-store delta SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_starter_slice_fixture_matrix_v1` | WHEN the starter slice is verified, THEN WCC, PageRank, and BFS fixtures SHALL pin projection, config, output carrier, semantic oracle, timing fields, target, and parity expectations. |

#### Similarity Is The First Relationship Bundle Slice

Pass 104 deepens the cleanest relationship-output candidate after the
WCC/PageRank/BFS starter slice: KNN and node similarity.

The core source shape is almost embarrassingly useful:

```text
SimilarityResult
  node1: long
  node2: long
  similarity: double

KnnResult
  HugeObjectArray<NeighborList>
  ranIterations
  didConverge
  nodePairsConsidered
  nodesCompared
  streamSimilarityResult(...)

SimilarityGraphResult
  similarityGraph
  comparedNodes
  isTopKGraph
  direction from graph schema
```

That maps naturally to a Knight Bus bundle:

```text
similarity_edge_score_bundle_v1:
  columns:
    source_internal_id
    target_internal_id
    score_f64

  sidecars:
    root_id_map
    original_id_map
    relationship_type
    score_property
    direction
    producer_kind: knn_stream | filtered_knn_stream | node_similarity_graph
    top_k
    top_n
    cutoff
    source_filter
    target_filter
    score_distribution_policy

  counters:
    compared_nodes
    relationship_count
    similarity_pair_count
    node_pairs_considered
    did_converge
    ran_iterations

  budget:
    graph_build_bytes
    bundle_bytes
    distribution_bytes
    resident_bytes
    mapped_bytes
    spill_bytes
```

The important architectural choice:

```text
Neo4j/GDS-compatible path:
  similarity stream
    -> SimilarityGraphBuilder
    -> SimilarityGraphResult
    -> RelationshipExporter
    -> database/result-store/mutate target

Knight Bus low-RAM path:
  similarity stream or graph result
    -> capped edge-score bundle
    -> optional exact distribution pass
    -> optional materializer to Neo4j-compatible relationship output
```

The product should not hide that choice. It should expose it:

| Mode | What User Gets | RAM Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `stream_only` | Neo4j-like rows with original ids and scores | lowest durable footprint, client consumes now |
| `bundle_exact` | external edge-score artifact plus receipt | predictable resident bytes, materialize later |
| `bundle_with_distribution` | bundle plus exact 14-key distribution | more post-processing cost, stronger parity |
| `gds_like_graph_build` | similarity graph first, then write/mutate/stats | highest compatibility, less RAM differentiation |
| `bounded_refuse_or_spill` | hard cap honored before graph/bundle build | slower or refused, but no surprise memory peak |

The pair-count admission formula is the first guardrail:

```text
max_pairs = n * (n - 1) / 2
if topN > 0:
  cap relationship count by topN
if topK > 0:
  cap average degree by topK-ish bound
estimate adjacency graph cost OR bundle cost before materialization
```

The subtle lifecycle issue is filtered KNN. The source itself carries a TODO
about splitting delegate/result state so only one of target filtering and KNN
result has to be retained. That is exactly the kind of small, concrete thing a
budget-bounded product should make visible:

```text
filtered similarity receipt:
  target-filtered?
  source filter predicate?
  result stream producer?
  target-filter producer?
  release point for unused producer?
  retained bytes before release?
  retained bytes after release?
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we say "KNN is just src,dst,score":
  we miss graph-build cost, distribution cost, id-map cost, filter retention,
  and mode-specific side-effect metadata.

If we say "we must clone GDS exactly":
  we may rebuild a similarity graph even when the user only wanted a bounded
  durable edge-score bundle.

If we expose both:
  compatibility users can choose GDS-like behavior, while cost-sensitive users
  can choose capped bundle behavior with explicit distribution/materialization
  tradeoffs.
```

The pass-104 product decision:

```text
After WCC/PageRank/BFS:
  implement KNN/similarity as the first relationship-output profile.

Do not start with path-finding path arrays.
Path arrays are the scarier memory problem, but KNN/similarity is the cleaner
proof that an algorithm-specific relationship bundle can preserve Neo4j-like
surface behavior while making RAM predictable.
```

New executable-spec candidates:

| Candidate | Contract |
|---|---|
| `profile_similarity_graph_build_receipt_v1` | WHEN a similarity stream is converted into a graph, THEN input graph id, compared nodes, root-id mapping, direction, relationship count, score property, top-k/full flag, graph-build bytes, and materialization target SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_pair_count_admission_v1` | WHEN KNN/node-similarity planning starts, THEN max pair count, topN cap, topK cap, cutoff, expected edge count range, RAM cap, selected profile, spill/refusal behavior, and estimate confidence SHALL be recorded before compute. |
| `profile_knn_edge_score_bundle_receipt_v1` | WHEN KNN emits similarity rows, THEN source id, target id, score, row order, score tolerance, reverse-edge policy, id-map sidecar, convergence fields, iteration count, and node-pairs-considered SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_mode_cost_matrix_v1` | WHEN stream/stats/write/mutate mode is selected, THEN requested columns, graph-build requirement, distribution requirement, side-effect metadata, output target, and expected extra bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_filter_lifecycle_receipt_v1` | WHEN filtered KNN runs, THEN source filter, target filter, chosen stream producer, retained producer objects, release point, and before/after retained bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_similarity_distribution_oracle_v1` | WHEN similarity distribution is requested, THEN min, max, mean, stdDev, p1, p5, p10, p25, p50, p75, p90, p95, p99, and p100 SHALL match the reference under declared tolerance. |
| `profile_similarity_fixture_matrix_v1` | WHEN the similarity slice is verified, THEN KNN, filtered KNN, node similarity, and filtered node similarity stream/stats/write/mutate fixtures SHALL pin rows, counters, distribution keys, graph equality, score tolerance, and one-row mode contracts. |

#### Path Finding Is The First Varlen Payload Slice

Pass 105 deepens the path-finding output family. This is where a naive
"relationship count times row size" memory estimate becomes dangerously wrong.

The smallest source-level carrier is:

```text
PathResult:
  index
  sourceNode
  targetNode
  nodeIds: long[]
  relationshipIds: long[]
  costs: double[]
  totalCost = costs[last]
```

The public stream row is bigger:

```text
PathFindingStreamResult:
  index
  sourceNode
  targetNode
  totalCost
  nodeIds: List<Long>
  costs: List<Double>
  path: optional Neo4j Path
```

And the write row is different again:

```text
ExportedRelationship:
  sourceNode
  targetNode
  values:
    totalCost: double
    optional nodeIds: long[]
    optional costs: double[]
```

This gives the first serious varlen artifact profile:

```text
path_route_bundle_v1:
  fixed columns:
    path_index
    source_internal_id
    target_internal_id
    total_cost_f64

  varlen bodies:
    node_ids_i64
    costs_f64
    optional_relationship_ids_i64

  offsets:
    node_ids_offset
    node_ids_len
    costs_offset
    costs_len

  sidecars:
    original_id_map
    algorithm
    subtype
    relationship_type
    write_node_ids
    write_costs
    path_requested
    path_created
    negative_cycle_mode
    result_store_target
    stream_close_status
```

The source evidence says path outputs have at least six subtypes:

| Subtype | Source Shape | First Storage Format | RAM Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| distance row | `source,target,distance` | fixed distance table | row count can be high, but no route arrays |
| endpoint-cost relationship | `source,target,totalCost` | edge-cost bundle | compact, mutate-friendly |
| route array stream | `nodeIds[]`, `costs[]` | varlen route bundle | array payload dominates |
| write route payload | `Value[]` with optional arrays | edge-cost plus optional varlen sidecars | flags decide payload size |
| random walk | `Stream<long[]>` -> `List<Long>` | walk node-list bundle | walks per node times walk length |
| virtual path object | `PathFactory.create(...)` | derived materializer, not default storage | object creation and node lookup overhead |

The important source-backed product rule:

```text
writeNodeIds defaults false
writeCosts defaults false

Therefore:
  full route persistence is already an opt-in surface.
  Knight Bus should make this explicit as a budget choice:
    endpoint-cost only
    endpoint-cost + node ids
    endpoint-cost + costs
    endpoint-cost + node ids + costs
```

The other source-backed warning is result-store eager collection:

```text
ShortestPathWriteStep:
  if result store target exists:
    relationshipStream.toList().stream()

Reason:
  a deferred path result stream would otherwise observe the terminated
  transaction flag and return empty.
```

For a bounded-RAM system, that is not an implementation detail. It is a product
contract:

```text
Before path result-store write:
  estimate number of paths
  estimate total nodeIds payload
  estimate total costs payload
  estimate boxed/list/path materialization if requested
  compare against cap
  choose:
    in-memory collect
    chunked spool
    mmap bundle
    refuse with exact reason
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
If we optimize only the algorithm state:
  route materialization can still blow the RAM cap after compute.

If we optimize only relationship count:
  six written relationships can hide six arrays of different lengths.

If we store every path as a Neo4j Path eagerly:
  we pay object and lookup cost even when the user only needs endpoint cost.

If we store a typed varlen route bundle:
  we can keep fixed columns compact, spill variable arrays early, and materialize
  Neo4j-compatible rows only when requested.
```

The pass-105 product decision:

```text
Path-finding should not be the first relationship-output proof.
KNN/similarity is cleaner.

But path-finding should be the first credibility proof for hard RAM caps:
  "I will spend more time, but never exceed 5 GB" is most meaningful when the
  output contains variable-length routes.
```

New executable-spec candidates:

| Candidate | Contract |
|---|---|
| `profile_path_result_varlen_carrier_receipt_v1` | WHEN a path algorithm produces route results, THEN source/target ids, route index, node-id length, cost length, relationship-id length, total cost, array-owner identity, clone policy, and stream close status SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_path_stream_materialization_receipt_v1` | WHEN stream output is produced, THEN yielded columns, original-id rewrite count, list boxing count, cost-list count, path requested/created/null status, and materialization bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_path_requested_column_budget_v1` | WHEN `nodeIds`, `costs`, `path`, or route fields are requested, THEN each requested column SHALL add an explicit estimated and measured byte budget before execution. |
| `profile_path_write_payload_option_receipt_v1` | WHEN write mode runs, THEN `writeNodeIds`, `writeCosts`, property key/type list, per-relationship payload bytes, and null/missing property behavior SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_path_result_store_eager_spool_receipt_v1` | WHEN result-store path output would eagerly collect a stream, THEN row count, payload bytes, cap, chosen in-memory/spill/mmap strategy, and refusal behavior SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_path_family_subtype_selector_v1` | WHEN path-finding is planned, THEN distance-row, endpoint-cost, route-array, random-walk, virtual-path, or negative-cycle subtype SHALL be selected before storage profile choice. |
| `profile_path_negative_cycle_receipt_v1` | WHEN Bellman-Ford detects negative cycles, THEN shortest-path-vs-negative-cycle selection, output row count, source/target self-cycle behavior, total cost, and write/mutate flag behavior SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_path_fixture_matrix_v1` | WHEN path-finding parity is verified, THEN all-shortest-path, Dijkstra, A*, Yen's, Bellman-Ford, and random-walk fixtures SHALL pin rows, route arrays, cost arrays, flag-null behavior, path object behavior, negative-cycle behavior, and relationship counts. |

#### Embeddings Are Matrix Outputs; ML Top-K Is A Later Lane

Pass 106 answers a narrow sequencing question left by pass 105: where do
embedding/vector outputs and ML top-k outputs belong in the verification spine?

The answer:

```text
WCC component vector
  -> PageRank score vector
  -> BFS node-list/path materialization
  -> embedding matrix output
  -> KNN/similarity edge-score bundle
  -> path route bundle
  -> KGE / ML top-k relationship output
  -> full link-prediction pipeline output
```

Why embeddings come before path routes:

```text
Embedding output size is large but mostly predictable:
  node_count * dimension * element_width

Path output size is less predictable:
  path_count * variable route lengths * selected payload columns
```

The source shape for embeddings is:

```text
node_embedding_matrix_v1:
  node_count
  dimension
  value_type:
    f32
    f64
    binary_bitset
  internal_storage:
    HugeObjectArray<FloatVector>
    NodePropertyValuesAdapter output
    HugeObjectArray<HugeAtomicBitSet>
  public_materializer:
    float[]
    double[]
    List<Double>
    node-property write/mutate
  sidecars:
    algorithm
    property_name
    mode
    original_id_map
    has_value_policy
    configuration
    loss_per_iteration_optional
```

The important source-backed detail is that the public API often expands or boxes
the compact carrier:

```text
Node2Vec / FastRP:
  float[] -> List<Double>

GraphSAGE:
  double[] -> boxed List<Double>

Binary embeddings:
  bitset -> dense double[] / float[] / long[]
```

This is exactly the Knight Bus design pattern:

```text
Store in the shape of compute.
Materialize in the shape of the API.
Receipt both.
```

For bounded RAM, the embedding matrix should not be eagerly converted into
per-row boxed lists unless the selected mode, requested columns, and cap allow
that materialization. A better implementation lane is:

```text
1. Store a typed matrix artifact.
2. Keep original-id mapping as a sidecar.
3. Page or stream rows under a declared cap.
4. Write or mutate through node-property target adapters.
5. Record actual matrix bytes and public-row materialization bytes separately.
```

KGE looks deceptively like KNN because the public row is also:

```text
sourceNodeId
targetNodeId
score
```

But source evidence says KGE has more provenance:

```text
TopKMapComputer:
  sourceNodes bitset
  targetNodes bitset
  nodeEmbeddingProperty
  relationshipTypeEmbedding
  scoreFunction
  topK
  concurrency
  candidate-link exclusion
  thread-local scorer
  TopKMap bounded queues
```

And write/mutate mode adds target materializers:

```text
write:
  TopKMap -> TopKGraph -> RelationshipExporter

mutate:
  TopKMap stream -> RelationshipsBuilder -> graphStore.addRelationshipType
```

So KGE can reuse the edge-score bundle, but only after the receipt grows:

```text
kge_topk_edge_score_bundle_v1:
  src_internal_id
  dst_internal_id
  score_f64
  topk_rank_optional
  source_filter_id
  target_filter_id
  node_embedding_property
  relationship_type_embedding_ref
  score_function
  candidate_exclusion_policy
  model_or_config_ref
  id_map_ref
```

Link-prediction pipelines are a later and heavier lane still. Their computation
path carries model catalog, trained pipeline model, graph-store filters,
classifier factory, execution context dependencies, user identity, progress
tracking, and exporter builders. They should stay out of the v1 implementation
spine unless model and pipeline provenance are first-class receipt fields.

Rubber duck check:

```text
If embeddings are treated like scalar node properties:
  dimension and boxing costs disappear from the plan.

If embeddings are stored as boxed lists:
  we lose the main RAM advantage before the algorithm result is even useful.

If KGE is treated as plain KNN:
  source/target candidate sets, model-derived scorer inputs, and existing-edge
  exclusion are under-specified.

If link prediction is pulled into v1:
  model catalog and pipeline provenance become blockers before the simpler
  edge-score bundle has been proven.
```

The pass-106 product decision:

```text
Embedding matrix is the next node-output proof after scalar vectors.
KNN/similarity is still the first relationship-output proof.
Path routes are the first hard varlen RAM proof.
KGE is the first ML top-k proof after KNN/similarity.
Full link prediction is later.
```

New executable-spec candidates:

| Candidate | Contract |
|---|---|
| `profile_node_embedding_matrix_receipt_v1` | WHEN an embedding algorithm finishes, THEN node count, dimension, value type, internal matrix owner, original-id map, property name, mode, and resident/mapped bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_embedding_value_type_receipt_v1` | WHEN embeddings are exposed as node-property values, THEN f32, f64, binary-bitset, dense materialization type, conversion policy, and first-value dimension caveat SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_binary_embedding_materializer_receipt_v1` | WHEN a binary embedding is materialized, THEN bitset bytes, dense target type, dimension, set-bit count, allocated output bytes, and materialization latency SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_embedding_stream_materialization_receipt_v1` | WHEN stream mode emits embeddings, THEN original-id mapping count, `hasValue` behavior, row count, list/boxing allocation estimate, selected columns, and stream high-water bytes SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_embedding_stream_write_mutate_parity_v1` | WHEN embedding stream/write/mutate parity is verified, THEN public rows, node-properties-written counts, write/mutate timings, graph-store residency, result-store target, and property value equality SHALL be pinned. |
