Rubber duck check:

```text
Can we reduce BFS RAM below GDS?
  The variable frontier lane is the obvious first lever. The fixed lanes remain
  a resident floor unless we intentionally change the algorithm profile.

Will bounded BFS be faster?
  Not necessarily. A bounded-frontier profile is primarily about predictable
  memory. It can be slower because it drains/syncs/spills more often.

Can we still be product-differentiated if slower?
  Yes, if the user chooses "finish under 5GB" or "reject before allocation"
  instead of surprise OOM. That is a different and valuable product promise.

What is the semantic trap?
  Returning the right set of nodes but wrong order, wrong target truncation,
  wrong path field, or wrong max-depth behavior. BFS is traversal-output
  sensitive, not just reachability-sensitive.
```

#### Dijkstra Weighted Paths Are Priority Frontier Plus Route Payload

Pass 134 deepens Dijkstra because it is the first path-finding family where
the memory story naturally splits into two independent products:

```text
distance product:
  source + weighted topology -> shortest distances

route product:
  source + weighted topology -> shortest distances
  plus predecessor state
  plus optional relationship ids
  plus route arrays
  plus optional Neo4j path object
  plus write/result-store materialization
```

That distinction matters more than the word "Dijkstra." A user often asks for
"shortest path", but the engine must know whether the user needs one scalar
distance, a predecessor tree, one explicit route, every route from one source,
or writeback relationships with `nodeIds` and `costs` properties. These are
different memory contracts.

GDS makes the estimate lane visible:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `priority queue` | `HugeLongPriorityQueue.memoryEstimation()` is always included. | Record heap/cost index bytes separately from graph topology. |
| `reverse path` | `HugeLongLongMap.memoryEstimation()` is always included for predecessors. | Route reconstruction has a predecessor floor even before output arrays. |
| `relationship ids` | Added only when `trackRelationships` is true. | Relationship-level path parity should be an explicit opt-in lane. |
| `targets bitset` | Added only for many-target mode. | One target, many targets, and all targets should be separate profiles. |
| `visited set` | Per-node bitset always included. | Settled-node accounting is a correctness and RAM floor. |
| `weight sidecar` | Runtime uses weighted relationship traversal. | Weighted topology capability must be verified before algorithm support flips. |
| `path arrays` | `pathResult` backtracks into node-id, relationship-id, and cost arrays. | Route payload is not free after distance computation. |
| `boxed stream rows` | Stream builder boxes primitive arrays into lists. | Public API compatibility can add object-allocation pressure. |
| `path object` | Stream builder may create a Neo4j `Path`. | Path materialization should be refused or receipted in strict mode. |
| `write payload` | Write step controls `totalCost`, `nodeIds`, and `costs` values through flags. | Write flags are memory and schema flags, not cosmetic options. |
| `result-store eager collection` | Write step collects paths eagerly when writing to result store. | Result-store mode may change peak memory and must be in the receipt. |

The pinned GDS memory fixtures are strong enough to become exact red tests:

| Graph Dimension | Relationship Tracking | GDS Dijkstra Estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 nodes | false | 40,616 bytes |
| 1,000 nodes | true | 56,832 bytes |
| 1,000,000 nodes | false | 40,125,488 bytes |
| 1,000,000 nodes | true | 56,125,704 bytes |
| 1,000,000,000 nodes | false | 40,131,104,128 bytes |
| 1,000,000,000 nodes | true | 56,133,545,800 bytes |

Many-target mode has its own bitset lane. The fixture pins 1,000 nodes without
relationship tracking at `40,616 + 168` bytes when `manyTargets` is true.

The runtime shape is:

```text
source/original id
  -> map to dense source id
  -> one target list OR AllTargets
  -> queue.add(source, 0.0)
  -> while queue not empty and termination running
      -> pop min-cost node
      -> visited[node] = true
      -> scan weighted relationships
      -> if target is not settled
          -> add target to queue
          -> or lower target cost
          -> update predecessor
          -> optionally update relationship id
      -> apply target policy
      -> maybe emit path
  -> pathResult backtracks predecessor tree
  -> stream/write layer maps ids and materializes payload
```

That gives us six honest Dijkstra/SSSP profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible resident one-target Dijkstra | Queue, visited, predecessor, optional relationship ids, one emitted route. | Fast when memory fits. | Baseline API parity. |
| Distance-only SSSP | Queue plus distance/visited state, but no public route arrays. | Faster output, lower payload memory. | Answer "how far" without building every path. |
| Lazy-route SSSP | Retain predecessor state but delay route arrays until requested. | Compute first, reconstruct routes on demand. | Useful when only a few routes are inspected. |
| Full-route stream | Retain and emit node/cost arrays for each reachable target. | Output can dominate compute. | GDS-compatible `nodeIds`, `costs`, `path` rows. |
| Write-total-cost-only | Write one relationship or relationship stream with only `totalCost`. | Lower payload than full write. | Honors `writeNodeIds=false` and `writeCosts=false`. |
| Strict-RAM bounded priority frontier | Cap queue/predecessor windows, spill or partition, or reject. | Potentially slower or unsupported depending on graph/weights. | Honest "run under this cap or refuse before OOM" mode. |

The strategic product implication:

```text
BFS proves frontier caps.
PageRank proves vector/message caps.
Dijkstra proves priority-frontier plus route-payload caps.
```

These are the first three algorithm state families a rewrite should document
and test before claiming broad Neo4j/GDS compatibility.

Recommended red-test order:

3. `test_dijkstra_many_target_bitset_is_accounted_now`
4. `test_dijkstra_request_carries_weight_and_target_config_now`

6. `fixture_dijkstra_graph1_single_source_path_set_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Dijkstra use less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, but only if we change the requested profile. Distance-only or lazy-route
  modes can avoid full path arrays and public object materialization. Strict-RAM
  modes can cap or spill frontier/predecessor state, but that is a different
  latency contract.

Will it be faster?
  Not automatically. The resident Rust path may improve some allocation and
  integration overheads, but the core algorithm still pays queue operations and
  weighted edge scans. The biggest predictable win is avoiding unnecessary route
  materialization or rejecting all-shortest-paths jobs that cannot fit.

What is the semantic trap?
  Returning the right total cost but the wrong ordered path, wrong flag-null
  behavior, wrong original-id mapping, or wrong result-store materialization.
  Dijkstra compatibility is path-payload sensitive.

What should the product say?
  "Choose your path payload and RAM cap before the run." That is clearer and
  more useful than promising every shortest-path call is both faster and lower
  RAM.
```

#### Bellman-Ford Turns Negative Edges Into A Detection Contract

Pass 135 deepens Bellman-Ford because it is the path-finding algorithm where
"shortest path" is not a sufficient product description. With Dijkstra, the
core contract is priority-frontier plus route payload. With Bellman-Ford, the
core contract is:

```text
source + weighted edge stream
  -> distance/predecessor/length vectors
  -> frontier and task-local queue windows
  -> repeated relax/sync phases
  -> negative-cycle detection
  -> either shortest-path rows
     or negative-cycle rows
     depending on mode and graph state
```

That shift matters for the RAM strategy. A user may only need to know that a
negative cycle exists. Another user may need the exact cycle as a public route.
Another may need normal shortest paths on graphs with negative weights but no
cycle. Those are not the same memory profile.

GDS exposes the state lanes cleanly:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `frontier` | Per-node `HugeLongArray` in the memory estimate and runtime. | Record global frontier bytes and iteration sizes. |
| `validBitset` | Per-node atomic bitset controls whether a node is already queued. | Record duplicate-suppression state separately from visited/settled semantics. |
| `distances` | `DistanceTracker` owns a huge atomic double array. | Distance state is mandatory for exact output. |
| `predecessors` | `DistanceTracker` owns a huge atomic long array. | Path and cycle reconstruction need predecessor state. |
| `lengths` | `DistanceTracker` owns a huge atomic long array and uses it as a lock. | Length is both correctness state and concurrency control. |
| `localQueue` | Each `BellmanFordTask` estimates a per-node local queue. | Bounded profiles should cap or shard task-local queue pressure. |
| `negativeCyclesVertices` | Optional huge long array when tracking negative cycles. | Detection-only and track-and-stream modes must be separate. |
| `negativeCycleIndex` | Runtime counter increments for detected cycles. | Receipts need detected count even when cycle payload is suppressed. |
| `route arrays` | `pathResult` and cycle builders emit node and cost arrays. | Public route rows should be a separate materialization lane. |
| `boxed stream rows` | Stream builder boxes arrays into lists and adds `isNegativeCycle`. | Stream compatibility can add output object pressure. |
| `write-negative-cycle flag` | Write config defaults false and makes tracking follow write intent. | Write mode should not silently track cycles unless the output mode needs it. |
| `stats flag` | Stats output includes `containsNegativeCycle`. | Detection should remain visible even when path payload is absent. |

The pinned GDS memory fixture is small but useful because it isolates the
negative-cycle tracking delta:

| Fixture Dimension | Track Negative Cycles | GDS Bellman-Ford Estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 nodes, 23 relationships, concurrency 4 | false | 1,400 bytes |
| 10 nodes, 23 relationships, concurrency 4 | true | 1,520 bytes |

The runtime shape is:

```text
source
  -> initialize frontier[source], validBitset[source], distance[source] = 0
  -> repeat while frontier is non-empty
      -> RUN: tasks claim 64-node frontier chunks
      -> scan weighted relationships
      -> tryToUpdate target distance/predecessor/length atomically
      -> enqueue changed targets into task-local localQueue
      -> detect lengthBound >= nodeCount + 1 as negative-cycle signal
      -> SYNC: append localQueue back to global frontier
  -> containsNegativeCycle = negativeCycleIndex > 0
  -> produceResult:
      if containsNegativeCycle:
        shortestPaths = empty
        negativeCycles = tracked cycle paths if configured
      else:
        shortestPaths = reconstructed paths if trackPaths
```

That gives six honest Bellman-Ford profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible stream | Distance/predecessor/length vectors, frontier/localQueue, route arrays, cycle selection. | Baseline compatibility when memory fits. | Match `gds.bellmanFord.stream`. |
| Detect-only negative-cycle mode | Distance/predecessor/length vectors plus detection counter, without cycle payload array. | Can stop earlier when cycle tracking is disabled. | Answer "is this graph invalid for shortest paths?" under a cap. |
| Track-and-stream cycle mode | Adds negative-cycle vertex tracking and route reconstruction. | More output work, but explains the cycle. | Emit `isNegativeCycle = true` rows. |
| Distance-only no-route mode | Retains distance vectors, skips public path arrays when route columns are not needed. | Lower output pressure. | Useful for scoring or planning without route payload. |
| Bounded frontier/localQueue mode | Caps or shards frontier and task-local queue windows. | Can be slower due to extra drain/sync/spill passes. | Finish under declared RAM or reject before allocation. |
| Write-negative-cycles mode | Tracks cycles only when write config asks to write them. | Avoids tracking cost in default write mode. | Preserve GDS write flag semantics. |

Recommended red-test order:

1. `test_bellman_ford_registered_but_unsupported_until_estimate_green_now`
2. `test_bellman_ford_estimate_matches_gds_negative_cycle_fixture_now`
3. `test_bellman_ford_request_carries_weight_and_cycle_config_now`
4. `fixture_bellman_ford_negative_edge_no_cycle_paths_v1`
5. `fixture_bellman_ford_negative_cycle_stream_oracle_v1`
6. `test_bellman_ford_cycle_detection_suppresses_shortest_paths_now`
7. `test_bellman_ford_track_negative_cycles_controls_cycle_payload_now`
8. `test_bellman_ford_write_negative_cycles_default_false_now`
9. `profile_bellman_ford_frontier_distance_receipt_v1`
10. `profile_bellman_ford_negative_cycle_receipt_v1`
11. `profile_bellman_ford_route_materialization_receipt_v1`
12. `profile_bellman_ford_bounded_frontier_window_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Bellman-Ford use less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, if the mode is narrower. Detect-only mode avoids storing cycle payloads,
  distance-only mode avoids public route arrays, and bounded frontier/localQueue
  mode can cap variable queue pressure. Exact full-route compatibility still
  needs distance, predecessor, and length lanes.

Will bounded Bellman-Ford be faster?
  Not necessarily. Bellman-Ford is usually chosen for negative-weight semantics,
  not raw speed. Bounded mode may be slower because it adds drain/sync/spill
  work. The product win is predictable memory and correct negative-cycle
  reporting under a declared cap.

What is the semantic trap?
  If a negative cycle exists, GDS suppresses normal shortest paths and switches
  stream selection to negative-cycle rows when tracking is enabled. Returning
  partial shortest paths in that case would look useful but be incompatible.

What should the product say?
  "Bellman-Ford is the negative-edge verifier. Choose detect-only, explain-cycle,
  distance-only, or full route payload before the run."
```

#### Delta-Stepping Is Bucketed Weighted SSSP With Range Admission

Pass 136 deepens Delta-Stepping because it is the weighted shortest-path
algorithm that turns the frontier into a bucketed parallel scheduling problem.
Dijkstra says "give me a priority queue." Bellman-Ford says "give me repeated
relaxation and negative-cycle semantics." Delta-Stepping says:

```text
source + weighted edge stream + delta
  -> distance/predecessor state
  -> shared frontier bin
  -> per-task local bins
  -> RELAX phase over current bin
  -> SYNC phase into next smallest non-empty bin
  -> route reconstruction for all reachable targets
```

That makes it one of the cleanest algorithm-shaped storage examples in GDS.
The shape is not a new durable graph store. It is canonical weighted topology
plus a bucketed scratch plane.

GDS exposes the state lanes:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `distance array` | Per-node huge atomic double array in the estimate. | Distance vector is mandatory for exact weighted SSSP. |
| `predecessor array` | Per-node huge atomic long array in the estimate and public runtime. | Public route output needs predecessor state. |
| `shared bin` | Range estimate: lower bound by node count, upper bound by relationship upper bound. Runtime allocates shared frontier by relationship count. | Admission should expose planned min/max and actual shared-frontier high water. |
| `local bins` | Range estimate: nodeCount/concurrency lower bound, concurrency*nodeCount upper bound. Runtime uses dynamic per-task `LongArrayList[]`. | Bucket pressure is concurrency and delta sensitive. |
| `delta` | Config default is `2.0` and fixture tests vary `0.25,0.5,1,2,8`. | Delta is a RAM/latency scheduling knob, not just an algorithm parameter. |
| `RELAX` phase | Tasks claim global frontier chunks of 64 and relax weighted relationships. | Record relax rounds, scanned edges, successful relaxations, and retries. |
| `SYNC` phase | Tasks copy their next local bin into the shared frontier. | Record sync rounds, next-bin selection, copied rows, and frontier size. |
| `local bin threshold` | Local phase continues while bin size is below 1000. | Threshold crossings should be visible in strict RAM mode. |
| `path arrays` | `pathResults` reconstructs node and cost arrays from predecessors. | Route payload remains path-family shared memory pressure. |
| `hand-written path result` | `DeltaSteppingPathResult` avoids generated array clones. | Clone/no-clone policy is part of output RAM evidence. |

The pinned GDS memory fixtures make the range admission concrete:

| Graph Dimension | Concurrency | GDS Delta-Stepping Estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 10,000 nodes, 100,000 relationships | 4 | 260,216..1,280,216 bytes |
| 100,000 nodes, 1,000,000 relationships | 4 | 2,600,216..12,800,216 bytes |

The runtime shape is:

```text
source
  -> frontier[0] = source
  -> distance[source] = 0
  -> create one task per concurrency
  -> currentBin = 0
  -> while currentBin != NO_BIN
      -> RELAX:
          tasks claim shared frontier in batches of 64
          if distance[node] >= delta * currentBin:
            scan weighted outgoing relationships
            atomically lower target distance/predecessor
            put target into localBins[floor(newDistance / delta)]
          while current local bin is non-empty and below threshold:
            clone local bin
            clear local bin
            relax cloned nodes
      -> choose smallest non-empty bin across all tasks
      -> SYNC:
          copy that local bin from each task into shared frontier
          clear local bin
      -> frontierSize = copied rows
  -> reconstruct all reachable paths from predecessor array
```

That gives six honest Delta-Stepping profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible all-shortest-paths Delta | Distance, predecessor, shared frontier, dynamic local bins, route arrays. | Fast enough when bucket memory fits and delta is reasonable. | Match `gds.allShortestPaths.delta.stream/write`. |
| Distance-only Delta | Distance plus shared/local bins, no predecessor or route payload. | Lower output and predecessor memory. | Answer distances when route payload is not needed. |
| Route-lazy Delta | Keep predecessor state, delay route arrays until requested. | Same compute, lower immediate output pressure. | Useful when only some routes are inspected. |
| Strict-bucket bounded Delta | Cap local bins and shared frontier, spill/drain between phases, or reject. | Potentially slower because of extra sync/spill. | Honest hard-RAM mode for weighted SSSP. |
| Delta-tuned planner mode | Choose delta from workload/hardware calibration. | Can improve bucket locality or reduce bucket explosion depending on graph. | Make delta a measured planning knob. |
| Cross-algorithm oracle mode | Run or compare against Dijkstra on fixtures/samples. | Extra verification time. | Prove exactness before claiming speed or RAM wins. |

Recommended red-test order:

1. `test_delta_stepping_registered_but_unsupported_until_estimate_green_now`
2. `test_delta_stepping_estimate_matches_gds_bucket_range_fixture_now`
3. `test_delta_stepping_request_carries_weight_delta_and_cap_now`
4. `fixture_delta_stepping_graph1_path_set_v1`
5. `test_delta_stepping_delta_values_do_not_change_exact_paths_now`
6. `test_delta_stepping_public_stream_requires_predecessor_state_now`
7. `test_delta_stepping_matches_dijkstra_random_powerlaw_oracle_now`
8. `profile_delta_stepping_bucket_estimate_receipt_v1`
9. `profile_delta_stepping_relax_sync_receipt_v1`
10. `profile_delta_stepping_bucket_window_receipt_v1`
11. `profile_delta_stepping_route_materialization_receipt_v1`
12. `profile_delta_stepping_strict_bucket_spill_or_reject_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Delta-Stepping use less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, but mostly by controlling bucket and output profiles. Distance-only can
  avoid predecessor/route payload. Strict-bucket mode can cap or spill shared
  frontier/local bins. Full GDS-compatible all-shortest-paths still needs
  predecessor and route materialization.

Will it be faster than Dijkstra?
  Sometimes, not as a blanket claim. Delta-Stepping can exploit parallel bucket
  relaxation, especially on suitable non-negative weighted graphs. The wrong
  delta or wide bucket pressure can erase the gain. The receipt should show
  delta, bucket high water, relax/sync rounds, and Dijkstra parity.

What is the semantic trap?
  Treating delta as approximate. GDS tests vary delta and still expect exact
  shortest-path results. Delta changes scheduling, not correctness.

What should the product say?
  "For weighted all-shortest-paths, choose a bucketed profile. We will show the
  estimated bucket range, observed bucket high water, route payload, and whether
  the run fit your cap."
```

#### Random Walk Makes Stochastic Output A Bounded Stream Contract

Pass 137 deepens Random Walk because it is the first path-finding family where
the output is stochastic, reproducible only under seed/source/concurrency
contracts, and naturally bounded by a stream buffer.

The core shape is:

```text
source nodes + seed + walk parameters + optional relationship weights
  -> dense source-node supplier
  -> optional cumulative-weight preprocessing
  -> concurrent walk producers
  -> task-local path buffer
  -> bounded blocking queue
  -> stream rows or count-visits mutate state
```

That makes Random Walk a strong fit for the product thesis, but only if we are
honest about what is being optimized. A streaming walk corpus, an aggregate
visit-count mutation, and a seeded deterministic test fixture are different
contracts.

GDS exposes the state lanes:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `walk parameters` | `WalkParameters` carries `walksPerNode`, `walkLength`, `returnFactor`, and `inOutFactor`. | The request must record every stochastic control knob. |
| `estimate parameters` | `WalkEstimateParameters` carries only `walkLength` and `walkBufferSize`. | The stream estimate is intentionally buffer-shaped, not full-result-corpus-shaped. |
| `walk queue` | `RandomWalk` allocates `ArrayBlockingQueue<>(walkBufferSize)`. | Queue capacity and queue high water are first-class RAM fields. |
| `walk payload` | Each emitted walk is a `long[]` path. | Walk length directly controls per-row payload bytes. |
| `task-local buffer` | `RandomWalkTask` allocates a `long[1000][]` staging buffer. | Per-task staging is a separate lane from the shared queue. |
| `backpressure` | `flushBuffer` offers to the queue with a 100ms timeout. | Bounded mode should record blocked offers and offer time. |
| `termination tombstone` | `runTasks` offers a zero-length tombstone after producers finish. | Stream lifecycle should record tombstone and termination reason. |
| `stream close` | `streamWalks(...).onClose(externalTerminationFlag::stop)`. | Early consumer close must stop producers. |
| `source nodes` | Empty source list walks all graph nodes; explicit source list maps original ids to dense ids. | Source policy, source count, and mapping hash need receipts. |
| `random seed` | Missing seed defaults to a generated long; fixed seed supports deterministic tests. | Seed presence/value/generated status is a correctness field. |
| `weighted preprocessing` | Weighted graphs validate non-negative weights and compute cumulative weights through degree centrality. | Weight validation and preprocessing bytes/time need a separate lane. |
| `stream result` | Stream builder maps dense ids to original ids and may create a `Path` with relationship type `NEXT`. | Path-object materialization remains optional output pressure. |
| `count visits` | Counting mode allocates per-node `HugeAtomicLongArray` and per-thread local walk state. | Count-visits is lower-output RAM but not walk-corpus output. |

The pinned GDS memory fixtures are small but precise:

| Mode | Fixture Dimension | Concurrency | GDS Random Walk Estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Stream walk corpus | walk length 80, walk buffer 1000, 100 nodes, 6000 relationships | 1 | 4,016..660,032 bytes |
| Count visits mutate | walk length 80, walk buffer 1000, 100 nodes, 6000 relationships | 1 | 1,496 bytes |
| Count visits mutate | walk length 80, walk buffer 1000, 100 nodes, 6000 relationships | 4 | 3,464 bytes |

The runtime shape is:

```text
config
  -> defaults: walkLength=80, walksPerNode=10, walkBufferSize=1000,
               returnFactor=1.0, inOutFactor=1.0
  -> validate weights are non-negative if a relationship property exists
  -> choose all nodes or explicit source-node list
  -> choose fixed seed or generate one
  -> build task supplier with graph.concurrentCopy()
  -> each task:
       next source node
       skip zero-degree source
       sampler.prepareForNewNode(source)
       repeat walksPerNode:
         path = sampler.walk(source)
         buffer path locally
         flush local buffer to bounded queue
  -> stream consumer:
       read queue until tombstone
       map dense ids to original ids
       optionally create Neo4j Path
       stop producers when stream closes
```

That gives six honest Random Walk profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible stream walks | Bounded queue, task-local walk buffers, long-array walk payloads, optional path objects. | Fast when consumer keeps up; backpressure when the queue is small. | Match `gds.randomWalk.stream`. |
| Strict-buffer stream | User-selected queue cap and possible slow producer flushes. | Slower under small caps or slow consumers. | Hard RAM bound for walk corpus output. |
| Count-visits mutate | Per-node visit counter plus per-thread local walk, no stored walk corpus. | Lower output pressure, aggregate result only. | Match aggregate `gds.randomWalk.mutate` semantics before exposing full corpus. |
| Seeded deterministic stream | Same stream lanes plus fixed seed and fixture-specific ordering/set policy. | Determinism may constrain parallel semantics. | Verification profile for exact fixtures. |
| Weighted random walk | Adds non-negative weight validation and cumulative-weight preprocessing. | More pre-processing before walks start. | Expose weighted admission and preprocessing cost. |
| Source-list local walk | Only selected start nodes, with original-to-dense mapping. | Lower work proportional to source list, but mapping must be exact. | Local/personal graph workloads where the user asks for walks around named seeds. |

Recommended red-test order:

1. `test_random_walk_registered_but_unsupported_until_estimate_green_now`
2. `test_random_walk_estimate_matches_gds_buffer_fixture_now`
3. `test_random_walk_counting_visits_estimate_matches_gds_fixture_now`
4. `test_random_walk_request_carries_seed_source_walk_and_buffer_config_now`
5. `test_random_walk_rejects_negative_relationship_weights_now`
6. `fixture_random_walk_seeded_stream_oracle_v1`
7. `fixture_random_walk_source_list_maps_to_dense_ids_now`
8. `test_random_walk_stream_path_matches_node_ids_now`
9. `test_random_walk_stream_close_stops_producers_now`
10. `profile_random_walk_queue_backpressure_receipt_v1`
11. `profile_random_walk_task_buffer_receipt_v1`
12. `profile_random_walk_weighted_preprocessing_receipt_v1`
13. `profile_random_walk_count_visits_receipt_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Random Walk use less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, especially in count-visits mode or strict-buffer stream mode. Count-visits
  avoids storing the walk corpus and keeps only per-node counters plus per-thread
  local walk state. Strict-buffer mode caps outstanding walk arrays.

Will it be faster?
  Not automatically. Smaller buffers can increase producer blocking, and weighted
  random walks pay preprocessing for cumulative weights. The predictable product
  win is a bounded walk-corpus contract with explicit backpressure, not a blanket
  speed claim.

What is the semantic trap?
  Random output is not free to reorder or vary silently. Seed, source mapping,
  concurrency, negative-weight rejection, stream close, and path-object parity
  are all correctness concerns.

What should the product say?
  "Random Walk is a bounded stochastic stream. Choose corpus, count-visits, or
  strict-buffer mode before the run, and we will show seed, source, weight,
  queue, and termination receipts."
```

#### Node2Vec Turns Walk Streams Into A Model-State Contract

Pass 138 deepens Node2Vec because it looks tempting to file it under Random Walk,
but that would hide the expensive part. Node2Vec is a stochastic walk generator,
a probability-cache builder, a compressed walk-corpus store, and a two-matrix
SGD trainer. The public result is an embedding vector per node, not the walks.

The core shape is:

```text
graph + seed + walk sampling config + training config
  -> validate non-negative relationship weights
  -> generate walks for all nodes
  -> register frequencies and sample count
  -> compress each walk into byte payloads
  -> build positive and negative sampling probability lanes
  -> initialize center and context embedding matrices
  -> train with positive window samples and negative samples
  -> stream/write/mutate node embedding vectors
```

This is why Node2Vec is one of the clearest "storage in the shape of the
algorithm" candidates. It has at least four independent memory products hiding
under one public procedure name:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `sampling config` | `Node2VecConfigTransformer` splits `SamplingWalkParameters` from `TrainParameters`. | The request must split walk sampling from SGD training. |
| `walk corpus estimate` | `nodeCount * walksPerNode` walks, each estimated as `long[walkLength]`. | Estimate parity starts before graph topology optimization. |
| `compressed walk corpus` | `CompressedRandomWalks` stores `HugeObjectArray<byte[]>` plus `HugeIntArray` lengths. | Compare against compressed GDS, not a raw walk matrix strawman. |
| `walk compression codec` | Each walk is delta encoded, zigzag encoded, then vlong encoded. | Round-trip tests and corpus-byte receipts are mandatory. |
| `iterator semantics` | Decompression reuses one `long[]` buffer and fills unused positions with `-1L`. | Consumers must not retain the shared buffer accidentally. |
| `probability cache` | Frequencies, positive sampling probabilities, and negative sampling distribution are per-node lanes. | Fused training still needs probability state or a changed verifier. |
| `embedding matrices` | Center and context embeddings are two per-node float-vector matrices. | Matrix residency is the floor unless we page, partition, quantize, or approximate. |
| `row initialization` | Rows are seeded from original node id plus random seed. | Original-id mapping and seed need fixture receipts. |
| `positive samples` | `PositiveSampleProducer` filters walk nodes, sets context windows, and emits center/context pairs. | Window size, filtering, and filtered-walk count belong in the receipt. |
| `negative samples` | `NegativeSampleProducer` binary-searches cumulative distribution values from a splittable RNG. | Negative distribution hash and RNG seed are correctness fields. |
| `SGD update` | `TrainingTask.run` updates embeddings after each positive sample and its negative samples. | Update order and task partitioning affect parity. |
| `stream output` | Stream converts float arrays into `List<Double>`. | Public streaming boxes embedding vectors and can dominate result materialization. |
| `write/mutate output` | Write/mutate use `FloatEmbeddingNodePropertyValues` and return loss rows. | Side-effect modes need artifact receipts separate from compute memory. |

The pinned GDS memory fixture is small enough to memorize:

| Fixture | Value |
|---|---:|
| nodes | 1,000 |
| walks per node | 10 |
| walk length | 80 |
| embedding dimension | 128 |
| concurrency | 1 |
| GDS estimate | 7,688,464 bytes |

The runtime shape is:

```text
config
  -> defaults: walkLength=80, walksPerNode=10, walkBufferSize=1000,
               returnFactor=1.0, inOutFactor=1.0,
               windowSize=10, negativeSamplingRate=5,
               positiveSamplingFactor=0.001,
               negativeSamplingExponent=0.75,
               embeddingDimension=128, iterations=1
  -> sourceNodes is ignored and treated as empty/all-node sampling
  -> validate weights are non-negative if a relationship property exists
  -> allocate compressed walk corpus with graph.nodeCount * walksPerNode slots
  -> concurrent tasks:
       choose next dense node
       skip degree-zero node
       sampler.prepareForNewNode(node)
       repeat walksPerNode:
         path = sampler.walk(node)
         register frequencies and sample count
         compressedWalks.add(index, path)
         periodically check termination after walkBufferSize paths
  -> after walk generation:
       build positive sampling probabilities
       build negative cumulative distribution
       initialize center/context embeddings from original id + seed
       for each iteration:
         partition compressed walks by sample count and concurrency
         emit positive center/context samples
         emit negative samples
         update center and context vectors in-place
         record loss
  -> output:
       stream all node embeddings as boxed doubles
       or write/mutate embedding vectors as node properties
```

That gives seven honest Node2Vec profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible compressed corpus | Compressed walk byte arrays, length array, probability cache, two embedding matrices. | Similar two-phase behavior: generate corpus, then train. | Match the public GDS mental model first. |
| Strict compressed-spill corpus | Keep only a bounded chunk of compressed walks resident; spill older chunks. | Slower if training rereads spilled chunks, but RAM cap is clear. | Budget-bounded exact-ish corpus handling, if IO receipts are strong. |
| Fused walk-to-training profile | Avoid storing all walks; generate chunks and train/aggregate as they pass. | Potentially lower RAM and better locality, but parity risk is real. | Differentiated profile only after seeded/statistical oracles pass. |
| Probability-only prepass | First pass registers frequencies/sample count, second pass trains from regenerated walks. | More walk generation work, much lower corpus residency. | Trade CPU for lower RAM while preserving sampling distributions. |
| Paged embedding matrices | Keep center/context rows paged or partitioned by node blocks. | Extra random access and update scheduling cost. | Necessary when matrices exceed the RAM cap. |
| Quantized/low-precision embeddings | Store rows in compressed precision with controlled decode/update windows. | Faster memory bandwidth, possible quality drift. | Approximate profile with quality/cosine receipts. |
| Stream/write materialization mode | Full embedding matrix plus boxed stream rows or node-property writes. | Result materialization can dominate for stream-all. | Public API parity and side-effect accounting. |

Recommended red-test order:

1. `test_node2vec_registered_but_p2_until_estimate_green_now`
2. `test_node2vec_estimate_matches_gds_default_fixture_now`
3. `test_node2vec_request_splits_sampling_and_training_params_now`
4. `test_node2vec_rejects_negative_relationship_weights_now`
5. `fixture_node2vec_seeded_single_thread_embedding_oracle_v1`
6. `fixture_node2vec_same_seed_same_concurrency_parity_v1`
7. `fixture_node2vec_same_seed_different_concurrency_relaxed_oracle_v1`
8. `test_node2vec_compressed_walk_round_trip_now`
9. `profile_node2vec_walk_corpus_receipt_v1`
10. `profile_node2vec_compressed_corpus_receipt_v1`
11. `profile_node2vec_probability_cache_receipt_v1`
12. `profile_node2vec_training_matrix_receipt_v1`
13. `profile_node2vec_stream_materialization_receipt_v1`
14. `profile_node2vec_spill_or_fused_walk_receipt_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Node2Vec use much less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, but the win is profile-specific. The walk corpus is the first target,
  especially if we spill, regenerate, or fuse it. GDS already compresses walks,
  so "less RAM" must beat compressed byte-array corpus residency, not raw walk
  arrays. The two embedding matrices remain the resident floor unless we change
  matrix storage.

Will it be faster?
  Not guaranteed. Fusing walks can improve locality and reduce allocation, but
  it can also change training order, random sampling, and convergence. Paged
  matrices reduce RAM but may add random IO. The right product claim is bounded
  memory with explicit quality/parity receipts, then measured latency.

What is the semantic trap?
  Treating Node2Vec as Random Walk output. In GDS, the walk corpus feeds a
  sampling and SGD training pipeline. Seeded single-threaded runs can be exact,
  but concurrent runs use cosine similarity tolerance. Our verifier should match
  that distinction.

What should the product say?
  "Node2Vec has independent walk-corpus, probability-cache, model-matrix, and
  output-materialization budgets. Choose exact compressed-corpus, bounded-spill,
  fused, or approximate matrix profile before the run, and we will show memory,
  seed, sample, loss, and similarity receipts."
```

#### Louvain Makes Coarsened Graph Generations The RAM Problem

Pass 139 deepens Louvain because it is the first mainstream community-detection
algorithm where the expensive state is not only a vector over the original graph.
Louvain repeatedly optimizes modularity, records a dendrogram level, and then
contracts the graph into a new community graph. That means the low-RAM design
problem is a sequence of graph generations, not a single adjacency format.

The core shape is:

```text
root graph + optional weight + optional seed + tolerance/maxIterations/maxLevels
  -> modularity optimization on the current working graph
  -> dendrogram level over original nodes
  -> summarize current graph into a community graph with summed weights
  -> repeat until unchanged node count, one node, convergence, or maxLevels
  -> stream/stats/write/mutate final communities, modularities, and optional paths through levels
```

The GDS estimator makes the storage problem unusually explicit:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `modularityOptimization()` | Per-node current/next communities, cumulative weights, node-community influences, atomic community weights, colors, seed mapping, and community-weight updates. | Treat optimizer state as a named live-state budget, not as hidden scratch. |
| `communityInfluences` map | Per-thread `LongDoubleHashMap(50)..LongDoubleHashMap(max(50,nodeCount))`; high-degree nodes allocate degree-sized maps. | Record high-degree tally map high water, spill/cap policy, and exactness. |
| `subGraph` | Rough range for a new CSR graph with one summed relationship property because Louvain creates a new graph every iteration. | Each contraction level should emit a generation receipt. |
| `dendrograms` | One `HugeLongArray` minimum; `maxLevels` arrays if intermediate communities are included, otherwise rolling two arrays. | Public output mode is a RAM decision before compute starts. |
| `seeding` | Optional reverse seed mapping and original-id seeding values across levels. | Seeded parity is a separate fixture from unseeded partition equivalence. |
| `output` | Stream rows carry `communityId` and optional `intermediateCommunityIds`; stats/write/mutate add modularity list, ran levels, distribution, timings, and side effects. | Result materialization is a distinct memory lane. |

The pinned estimator fixture is important because it shows why one memory number
is misleading:

| Nodes | Relationships | Concurrency | Max Levels | Include Intermediate | GDS Estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 1 | 1 | true | 6,414,145..23,057,704 bytes |
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 1 | 10 | true | 6,414,145..30,258,064 bytes |
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 1 | 10 | false | 6,414,145..23,857,744 bytes |
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 4 | 10 | true | 6,417,433..36,258,328 bytes |
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 42 | 10 | true | 6,459,081..112,261,672 bytes |
| 100,000 | 500,000 | 42 | 10 | false | 6,459,081..105,861,352 bytes |

That gives seven honest Louvain profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible full intermediate | Keep modularity state, contracted subGraph, and every dendrogram level needed for intermediate output. | Similar public semantics; high memory when concurrency and levels grow. | First compatibility target for stream/stats/write/mutate parity. |
| Rolling final-community mode | Keep only current/previous dendrogram arrays when intermediate communities are not requested. | Same final-community semantics; lower output-state RAM. | Default low-RAM exact mode for final partition workloads. |
| Spillable contracted generations | Persist each aggregate community graph generation as a bounded artifact instead of fully retaining it. | Slower if reads hit disk, but peak resident state is bounded. | The cleanest "contracted graph sidecar" implementation. |
| Exact spill tally maps | Spill high-degree `communityInfluences` maps when a per-task budget is exceeded. | Slower on supernodes; exact if sorted/merged deterministically. | Budget-bounded modularity optimization. |
| Heavy-node split tally | Split high-degree nodes into deterministic edge chunks and reduce community tallies. | Extra reduce step; lower per-thread spikes. | Better for skewed fraud/KG graphs with supernodes. |
| Warm-start delta Louvain | Reuse prior generation/community state and update only affected regions when graph changes. | Potentially much faster for recurring jobs; correctness is harder. | PMF-heavy nightly-batch story: "remember yesterday." |
| Stats-only / stream-only output | Choose profile from requested output columns and side effects. | Avoids unneeded intermediate IDs, write payloads, or distributions. | Lets planner convert public API shape into a storage plan. |

Recommended red-test order:

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Louvain use much less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, in specific modes. Rolling dendrogram mode removes full intermediate
  community arrays when the user only needs final communities. Spillable graph
  generations and high-degree tally spilling can bound peak resident state.
  But the modularity state, community arrays, and contracted graph still exist
  conceptually; they move between resident, chunked, and durable artifact forms.

Will it be faster?
  Not automatically. Exact spill paths can be slower than keeping everything in
  memory. The faster opportunity is recurring Louvain: warm-start yesterday's
  community/generation state, limit work to affected regions, and prove the
  result with modularity/partition receipts.

What is the semantic trap?
  Raw community ids are not the same as partition correctness. Fixtures should
  compare partition equivalence, modularity tolerance, level count, and explicit
  seed/consecutive-id behavior. Also, `includeIntermediateCommunities` is not a
  display option; it changes memory planning.

What should the product say?
  "Louvain has optimizer-state, tally-map, contracted-generation, dendrogram,
  and output budgets. Choose final-only, full-intermediate, spillable, or
  warm-start mode before the run, and we will show generation-by-generation RAM,
  modularity, stop, and partition receipts."
```

#### Leiden Adds A Refinement Contract On Top Of Louvain's Shape

Pass 140 deepens Leiden because it is PMF-relevant for GraphRAG-style community
pipelines and it is easy to misunderstand as "newer Louvain, same storage." The
evidence says something more useful: Leiden keeps the contracted-generation
shape, but adds local move, refinement, and aggregation state to guarantee better
community connectedness. That makes it a stronger verifier target and a more
interesting low-RAM profile family.

The core shape is:

```text
root graph + gamma/theta + tolerance + random seed + optional seed property
  -> initialize singleton/seeded local-move communities and volume arrays
  -> local move phase with global queue, local queues, and community maps
  -> modularity computation and tolerance/decrease checks
  -> update output dendrogram
  -> refinement phase with singleton bitset, probabilities, merge tracking, and random seed
  -> graph aggregation phase into a summed community graph
  -> maintain partition for the next iteration
  -> stream/stats/write/mutate communities, convergence, modularity, and optional intermediate communities
```

The important distinction from Louvain is that Leiden's estimator is phase
structured:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `local move base arrays` | Local-move communities, node volumes, community volumes, and current communities. | Treat community and volume arrays as named phase state. |
| `seeded communities` | Added only when `seedProperty` is present. | Seed support changes both correctness and RAM. |
| `local move phase` | Community weights, atomic community volumes, global queue, global queue bitset, per-task community map, and local queue. | Queue high water and swap/requeue behavior need receipts. |
| `refinement phase` | Encountered communities, probabilities, merged volumes, relationships between communities, refined communities, and merge bitset. | This is the well-connectedness contract and should not be hidden. |
| `aggregation phase` | Aggregated CSR graph range, sorted communities, and atomic coordination array. | Each generation needs graph bytes plus sorting/coordination bytes. |
| `post-aggregation phase` | Next local-move communities, next volumes, and community-to-node map. | Cross-level transition state needs its own budget. |
| `dendrogram/output` | Dendrogram manager tracks final or intermediate output; public stream can emit intermediate community ids. | Output mode changes resident state. |

The pinned memory fixture is:

| Nodes | Relationships | Concurrency | Seed | Include Intermediate | Max Levels | GDS Estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| 101,000 | 100,000 | 1 | none | false | 3 | 18,361,384..25,830,376 bytes |
| 101,000 | 100,000 | 4 | none | false | 3 | 20,789,008..34,314,976 bytes |

That gives seven honest Leiden profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible phase pipeline | Keep all local-move, refinement, aggregation, dendrogram, and output state needed for public parity. | Similar phase sequence to GDS; best compatibility baseline. | First correctness target. |
| Final-only rolling dendrogram | Avoid intermediate dendrogram materialization when only final communities are requested. | Same final output with lower output-state RAM. | Default exact low-RAM public stream/stats mode. |
| Bounded local-move queues | Cap/spill local queues and community maps by node-degree/community-count pressure. | Slower under high churn, but queue memory is predictable. | Good for skewed graphs with repeated neighbor requeue. |
| Spillable refinement workspace | Spill encountered-community/probability/merge state for large communities. | Slower refinement; exact if merge order and RNG are deterministic. | The Leiden-specific low-RAM differentiator. |
| Spillable aggregation generations | Store aggregate community graphs as sidecar artifacts by level. | Slower if later phases read on-file graph chunks. | Shared with Louvain, but with sorted-community receipts. |
| Warm-start delta Leiden | Reuse prior communities and aggregate generations across recurring runs. | Potentially much faster for recurring GraphRAG/fraud batches; hard verifier. | PMF-heavy recurring compute path. |
| Approximate bounded refinement | Cap refinement/probability work and declare approximation. | Lower RAM and perhaps faster; output quality can drift. | Only valid with explicit quality/modularity/partition receipts. |

Recommended red-test order:

1. `test_leiden_registered_but_p2_until_estimate_green_now`
2. `test_leiden_estimate_matches_gds_phase_fixture_now`
3. `test_leiden_request_carries_gamma_theta_seed_and_level_config_now`
4. `test_leiden_forbids_intermediate_communities_with_consecutive_ids_now`
5. `fixture_leiden_small_two_community_oracle_v1`
6. `fixture_leiden_tolerance_modularity_oracle_v1`
7. `fixture_leiden_local_move_karate_oracle_v1`
8. `fixture_leiden_refinement_karate_oracle_v1`
9. `test_leiden_seed_modes_match_gds_now`
10. `profile_leiden_estimate_lanes_receipt_v1`
11. `profile_leiden_local_move_queue_receipt_v1`

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can Leiden use much less RAM than GDS?
  Yes, but the easiest true win is output-state and artifact-state bounding:
  final-only dendrogram, spillable aggregate generations, and bounded local
  queues. The more Leiden-specific win is refinement workspace bounding, but
  that is also where exactness and random-seed behavior are most fragile.

Will it be faster?
  Not by default. Leiden has more phases than Louvain. A same-run exact bounded
  profile may be slower if it spills refinement or aggregation state. The speed
  story is stronger for recurring jobs where prior communities/generations let
  the run avoid full recompute.

What is the semantic trap?
  Treating Leiden as Louvain with a different name. Leiden's promise is
  well-connected communities, and the refinement phase is central to that. A
  verifier that only checks final community rows can miss broken local-move or
  refinement semantics.

What should the product say?
  "Leiden has local-move, refinement, aggregation, dendrogram, and output
  budgets. Choose exact, bounded-local-move, spill-refinement, spill-aggregation,
  or warm-start mode before the run, and we will show phase-level RAM,
  convergence, modularity, and partition receipts."
```

#### NodeSimilarity Is A Candidate-Pair Budget Contract

Pass 141 deepens NodeSimilarity because it is the clearest example of the
problem the product wants to be famous for: a useful graph algorithm whose naive
shape wants to become all-pairs, but whose practical shape can be bounded by
degree gates, filters, components, topK/topN, and explicit candidate strategy.
This is not just "make the graph smaller." It is "do not let pair generation
become an unbounded hidden materializer."

The core shape is:

```text
graph + metric + similarity cutoff + degree bounds + source/target filters
  + component policy + topK/topN/bottomK/bottomN + output mode
  -> prepare neighbor vectors and optional weight vectors
  -> optionally compute/use components to prune target ranges
  -> scan source-target candidate pairs
  -> compute weighted or unweighted vector similarity
  -> skip NaN similarities but retain zero similarities that pass gates
  -> maintain per-node topK queues and/or global topN queue
  -> optionally materialize a similarity graph
  -> stream/write/mutate source-target-similarity rows
```

The important memory lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `node filter` | Per-node bitset/long-array lane in the memory estimator. | Record source/target filter population and bytes before candidate planning. |
| `vectors` | Per-node `HugeObjectArray<long[]>` neighbor vectors using average degree. | The vector-prep budget is separate from candidate-pair budget. |
| `weights` | Optional per-node `HugeObjectArray<double[]>` with `0..max` range. | Weighted mode must pay a different floor and verify weight-vector alignment. |
| `components/WCC` | Sorted nodes, upper bound per component, WCC or component mapping. | Component pruning is both correctness input and candidate-count reducer. |
| `topK map` | Per-source-node bounded priority queues through `TopKMap`. | Bounded memory needs per-node queue capacity and ownership receipts. |
| `topN list` | One bounded global pair queue through `TopNList`. | Global topN is a different product from per-node topK. |
| `similarity graph` | `SimilarityGraphBuilder` estimates/builds a `HugeGraph` adjacency list. | Full graph materialization must be an explicit admission decision. |
| `filtered variant` | Filtered estimator delegates to normal estimator, config adds source/target filters. | Filtering changes candidate semantics even when estimator class is shared. |

The pinned memory fixtures are:

| Nodes | Relationships Upper Bound | Mode | GDS Estimate Facts |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1,000,000 | 5,000,000 | topK 10, weighted estimate enabled | node filter `125,016`, vectors `56,000,016`, weights `16..56,000,016`, topK map `248,000,016`; total implied `304,125,072..360,125,072` bytes |
| 1,000,000 | 5,000,000 | topK 100, weighted estimate enabled | same filter/vector/weight lanes, topK map `1,688,000,016`; total implied `1,744,125,072..1,800,125,072` bytes |
| 1,000,000 | 5,000,000 | topK plus topN 100 | topN list adds `2,504` bytes on top of the matching topK fixture |
| 100 | 20,000 | topK and topN greater than node count | `570,592..732,192` bytes |
| 1,000,000 | 5,000,000 | components | sorted-by-component `8,000,040`, upper-bound-per-component `8,000,040`, and either component mapping `8,000,040` or WCC `8,000,064` bytes in the fixture |

That gives eight honest NodeSimilarity profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible topK map | Materialize vectors/weights, scan candidates, keep per-source bounded queues. | Fast when all vectors fit and pruning is good; can still scan many pairs. | First compatibility target for common recommendation workloads. |
| Strict candidate-budget reject | Refuse when degree/filter/component analysis predicts too many pairs for the RAM cap. | Fast failure before surprise O(n^2) work. | The cleanest PMF promise: predictable admission. |
| Component-pruned exact | Partition candidate scans by WCC/component property and never compare across components. | Faster and lower RAM when components are many/small. | Exact if component policy matches GDS semantics. |
| Filter-pushdown exact | Apply source and target filters before vector prep and candidate scan where safe. | Faster/lower RAM for targeted recommendations/entity matching. | Strong because GDS currently notes prep work can still happen for unused nodes. |
| Spillable topK queues | Keep bounded in-memory queues and spill candidate batches or loser queues under pressure. | Slower under high-degree/high-candidate graphs, exact if merge order is deterministic. | RAM-bounded exact mode. |
| Blocked vector-slice scan | Store sorted neighbor vectors in chunked/compressed slices and scan blocks under a memory cap. | Extra decompression/read passes; predictable high-water bytes. | Useful for large graphs where vector residency is the floor. |
| Stream-only no graph materialization | Emit rows/topK/topN without building a `HugeGraph` unless the user asks. | Lower peak RAM; output consumer may become backpressure source. | Default product posture. |
| Approximate sketch/LSH | Use MinHash/LSH/similarity sketches to bound candidates before exact refinement or as approximate result. | Often faster/lower RAM; not GDS-compatible unless exact refinement covers recall. | Separate approximate profile with quality receipts, never hidden behind exact API. |

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can NodeSimilarity use much less RAM than a naive implementation?
  Yes. The product can avoid all-pair materialization, cap topK/topN outputs,
  prune by filters/components, and reject or spill when predicted candidate
  count exceeds the RAM cap. This is a genuine bounded-compute story.

Can it use much less RAM than GDS?
  Sometimes. GDS already uses bounded topK/topN structures, so the truthful
  wins are earlier/lazier vector prep, stronger filter pushdown, explicit
  component pruning, spillable queue/vector state, stream-first output, and
  pre-run refusal instead of hidden expansion.

Will it be faster?
  Only when pruning is strong or output materialization is avoided. A strict
  low-RAM exact profile can be slower because it spills or scans in blocks. An
  approximate sketch profile can be faster, but it is no longer the same exact
  GDS contract unless exact refinement proves recall.

What is the semantic trap?
  Treating source and target filters as symmetric, forgetting bottomK/bottomN
  sign semantics, dropping zero similarities that GDS emits, comparing across
  components when component mode forbids it, or parallelizing topK writes without
  preserving one-queue-owner-per-source.

What should the product say?
  "NodeSimilarity is admitted as a candidate-pair budget. We will tell you
  before the run whether it will fit, whether it will spill, which exact or
  approximate profile is selected, and how many pairs/vectors/queues were
  actually materialized."
```

#### KNN Turns Similarity Into An Iterative Neighbor-List Contract

Pass 142 narrows KNN away from generic "similarity search" and into the actual
state machine GDS runs: initialize bounded neighbors, repeatedly split old/new
neighbors, reverse those deltas, join candidate pairs, add random joins, mutate
per-node topK lists, and stop by convergence threshold or iteration limit. That
shape matters because it shows where lower RAM is credible and where it is just
wishful thinking.

The core shape is:

```text
graph + property specs + topK + sampleRate + deltaThreshold
  + sampler + random seed + randomJoins + filters + similarity cutoff
  -> derive boundedK, sampledK, maxUpdates, and updateThreshold
  -> initialize one compact NeighborList per node from random candidates
  -> repeat until maxIterations or updateCount <= updateThreshold
    -> split checked neighbors into old and unchecked sampled neighbors into new
    -> reverse old and new neighbor lists
    -> join new-new and new-old candidate pairs
    -> perform configured random joins
    -> mutate per-node bounded NeighborList instances
  -> optionally filter below similarity cutoff
  -> stream/stats/write/mutate source-target-score rows plus convergence counters
```

The important memory and correctness lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| `top-k-neighbors-list` | Per-node `HugeObjectArray<NeighborList>`; each list stores score/id pairs as a `long[2 * topK]`. | This is durable resident state and should usually stay resident in exact mode. |
| `old-neighbors` and `new-neighbors` | Per-iteration `HugeObjectArray<LongArrayList>` lanes created from checked/un-checked neighbor state. | These are prime candidates for reuse, cursorization, shard-local buffers, or spill. |
| `old-reverse-neighbors` and `new-reverse-neighbors` | Per-iteration reversed lists built from old/new lists. | Reverse construction needs pair-count and replay receipts if made streaming. |
| Initial sampler | Uniform sampler or random-walk sampler, priced per thread. | Sampler type is a real RAM/latency/quality knob. |
| Sampled-random buffer | Per-thread open-hash container sized by sampledK. | Record sampledK and hash-cache bytes before admission. |
| Neighbor mutation | `NeighborList.add` handles duplicate rejection, priority ordering, perturbation, checked bits, and insertion-count return. | A custom Rust carrier must preserve these semantics before claiming compatibility. |
| Join counters | Random joins increment pair counters but are not counted in update convergence. | Receipts must separate updates, random joins, and total pairs considered. |
| Filtered target queues | Filtered KNN can short-circuit via target seeding and bounded target queues. | Producer-path and release receipts can reduce retained state. |
| Output materialization | Stream/stats/write/mutate paths expose rows, distributions, relationship writes, and graph equality. | Public mode changes memory; stream-first should not silently pay graph-materialization costs. |

The cleanest product profiles are:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible uniform KNN | Resident per-node topK lists, four temp list ranges, uniform sampler buffers. | Baseline compatibility target; good tiny-fixture parity first. | Exact-ish GDS-compatible approximate KNN behavior with stable public rows/counters. |
| Random-walk-seeded KNN | Adds random-walk sampler state, cache, and fallback sampling. | May reduce later iterations, but sampler itself is heavier. | User chooses better initialization versus sampler RAM/latency. |
| Temp-list reuse exact | Reuse old/new/reverse arrays across iterations where semantics allow. | Potentially faster and lower allocation churn. | Directly follows GDS source TODOs; low-risk optimization to benchmark. |
| Spillable delta-list exact | Keep resident topK lists in memory; spill/cursor old/new/reverse deltas by shard. | Slower under pressure; exact if replay/candidate order is proven. | Best low-RAM story for large graphs with bounded peak memory. |
| Filtered target-owned result | For target-filtered runs, emit from target-filtering queues and release unused KNN result state. | Faster/lower RAM when target set is small or seeding is optimal. | Turns filtered KNN lifecycle into a real storage profile. |
| Stream-only edge-score bundle | Emit compact `src,dst,score` rows without building a full similarity graph. | Lower peak RAM; downstream consumer may be bottleneck. | First relationship-output slice for product demos. |
| Strict admission/reject | Estimate temp lists, sampler, output mode, and property plane before work starts. | Fast fail when a cap cannot admit the run. | The PMF promise: no surprise candidate explosion. |
| Approximate candidate sketch | Use LSH/MinHash/vector quantization to reduce candidate generation, then optionally exact-refine. | Often faster and lower RAM, but not the same contract unless recall is proven. | Separate approximate mode with quality receipts, never hidden behind exact API. |

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can KNN use much less RAM than a naive implementation?
  Yes. It avoids all-pair result materialization by keeping bounded per-node
  neighbor lists and only sampling/joining candidates. A naive all-pair
  similarity matrix is the wrong baseline for this algorithm.

Can it use much less RAM than GDS?
  Sometimes, but not by replacing the compact `NeighborList`. GDS already has a
  compact resident carrier. The source-backed opportunities are temp-list reuse,
  cursorized/spillable old-new-reverse deltas, filter-producer release,
  stream-only edge-score output, property-plane compression, and up-front
  admission/reject.

Will it be faster?
  Not automatically. Spillable exact mode may be slower. Uniform sampler can be
  cheaper but may need more iterations. Random-walk sampler can cost more up
  front but may improve candidate quality. The honest speed story is profile
  selection plus receipts, not "Rust will make KNN fast."

What is the semantic trap?
  Random joins are counted as pairs considered but not as convergence updates.
  `NeighborList` uses checked-bit mutation inside stored element ids. Source and
  target filters are not interchangeable. Random seed and concurrency have
  constraints. All of those must be tests, not prose.

What should the product say?
  "KNN has a resident topK neighbor budget and a temporary candidate-delta
  budget. Choose exact compatible, lower-RAM spill/reuse, filtered target,
  stream-only, or approximate mode before the run, and we will show where every
  byte and every candidate pair went."
```

#### FastRP Makes Dense Embeddings The Budget

Pass 143 turns FastRP from an "embedding algorithm" label into a very concrete
storage problem. GDS FastRP is not mainly about frontier state or candidate
pairs. It is about dense vectors: one final output matrix, two propagation work
matrices, and an optional property-vector table. That makes it one of the
cleanest tests of whether Knight Bus can be honest about RAM caps while still
matching Neo4j/GDS semantics.

The core shape is:

```text
graph + featureProperties + relationshipWeightProperty
  + embeddingDimension + propertyRatio + iterationWeights
  + nodeSelfInfluence + normalizationStrength + randomSeed
  -> derive propertyDimension and baseEmbeddingDimension
  -> allocate propertyVectors[featureCount][propertyDimension]
  -> allocate final embeddings[nodeCount][embeddingDimension]
  -> allocate embeddingA[nodeCount][embeddingDimension]
  -> allocate embeddingB[nodeCount][embeddingDimension]
  -> build degree partitions
  -> initialize property random vectors
  -> initialize deterministic node random vectors in embeddingB
  -> optionally add normalized self-influence into final embeddings
  -> for each iterationWeight:
       current = embeddingA or embeddingB
       previous = the other buffer
       scan neighbors
       combine weighted or unweighted previous vectors
       degree-normalize current
       L2-normalize current
       add iteration-weighted current into final embeddings
  -> stream/write/mutate dense vectors or emit stats metadata
```

The important memory and correctness lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Final `embeddings` | `FastRPResult` owns `HugeObjectArray<float[]> embeddings`; stream/write/mutate adapt it into public rows or side effects. | This should usually become an artifact sidecar, not a boxed public row representation. |
| `embeddingA` | Full per-node float-vector work buffer used as current or previous by iteration parity. | Candidate for chunking/spill, but neighbor propagation needs previous vectors available by target id. |
| `embeddingB` | Full per-node float-vector work buffer; initially stores deterministic random node vectors. | Recompute-versus-spill tradeoff must preserve original-id seed behavior. |
| `propertyVectors` | Fixed table sized by feature input count and property dimension. | Small but semantic; receipt must include feature offset map and property-tail hash. |
| Feature-property tail | Property projection adds scalar/array features into trailing dimensions. | Compression must preserve scalar/array equivalence and missing-value errors. |
| Relationship weights | Weighted combiner uses relationship property and throws on missing weight when configured. | Weighted profile needs explicit missing-weight failure tests and fallback policy. |
| Degree partitions | Runtime partitions by degree before propagation. | Chunking should expose partition sizes, edge counts, and replay count. |
| Output materialization | Stream emits original id plus vector rows; write/mutate store node properties; stats emits metadata. | Public mode must not be mistaken for storage mode; row boxing/list bytes need separate receipts. |

The cleanest product profiles are:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible resident FastRP | Final matrix plus A/B work matrices plus property vectors all resident. | Fastest exact-compatible baseline, highest peak RAM. | Establishes correctness parity before innovation. |
| Sidecar-final resident-work FastRP | Keep A/B resident; write final embeddings to an mmap/direct sidecar as chunks complete. | Slightly slower output, similar propagation speed. | Reduces heap pressure while preserving fast neighbor propagation. |
| Chunked propagation FastRP | Partition A/B into vector pages with an edge-aware cache for neighbor reads. | Slower and more complex; exact if page replay is deterministic. | Bounded peak RAM for large graphs where 3x dense matrices are impossible. |
| Recompute-random-vector FastRP | Do not keep all initial random vectors after they are no longer needed; recompute from seed/original id when useful. | Trades CPU for lower retained state; best when iterations and graph degree make recompute cheaper than spill. | Uses FastRP's deterministic seed rule as a RAM lever. |
| Property-tail compressed FastRP | Store base and property dimensions separately; compress sparse or low-entropy property tail. | Extra decode cost during propagation. | Best for feature-heavy graphs where propertyRatio is high but feature tails are sparse. |
| Stats-only/admission FastRP | Run estimator and config validation without dense output materialization. | Fast fail or cheap planning. | Product promise: tell the user before the run if dense embeddings cannot fit. |
| Quantized approximate FastRP | Store vectors as int8/fp16 blocks with exact or approximate cosine/loss caveats. | Often faster/lower RAM, but no longer exact GDS parity unless refinement proves tolerance. | A separate approximate mode, not hidden behind the exact API. |
| Stream-window materializer FastRP | Keep durable matrix sidecar; stream rows in bounded pages and avoid giant boxed lists. | Lower peak memory; stream consumer can dominate wall time. | Makes the public Cypher row contract safe for large embeddings. |

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can FastRP use much less RAM than a naive implementation?
  Yes. A naive implementation might materialize extra row objects, boxed vectors,
  duplicate matrices, or full stream rows. The GDS shape is already more
  disciplined: one final dense matrix plus two work matrices plus optional
  property vectors.

Can it use much less RAM than GDS?
  Sometimes. GDS's exact resident path intentionally pays for three dense
  embedding lanes. Knight Bus can reduce heap or peak RAM by sidecar-writing the
  final matrix, chunking A/B propagation buffers, recomputing deterministic
  initial vectors, compressing property tails, or materializing stream rows in
  windows. The honest tradeoff is slower propagation or output for a tighter cap.

Will it be faster?
  Resident exact mode can be competitive if Rust improves allocation, vector
  layout, cache locality, and row materialization. Bounded-spill exact mode is
  likely slower than resident GDS. Quantized or approximate modes can be faster,
  but they must be labeled approximate unless fixtures prove exact tolerance.

What is the semantic trap?
  Random vectors are seeded by original node id, not just mapped id. Property
  ratio changes the base/property dimension split. Scalar and array feature
  inputs must align. Missing feature properties fail during random-vector init.
  Missing relationship weights fail when weighted propagation sees NaN. Stats
  mode should not become a loophole that hides dense computation.

What should the product say?
  "FastRP is a dense-vector budget. We will show the final matrix, A/B work
  buffers, property vectors, and output materializer separately. Choose resident
  fast, bounded-spill exact, sidecar output, or approximate compressed mode
  before the run."
```

#### GraphSAGE Turns Embeddings Into A Model-And-Batch Budget

Pass 144 deepens GraphSAGE because it is the first embedding family where the
word "embedding" is actively misleading. FastRP is dense matrix plus propagation
buffers. Node2Vec is walk corpus plus model state. GraphSAGE is a trained model
artifact, a feature plane, sampled subgraphs, a computation graph, optimizer
state, gradient state, and a dense embedding output. It is not one storage
format. It is a family of budgets.

The core shape is:

```text
train:
  graph + featureProperties + sampleSizes + aggregator + activation
    + batchSize + searchDepth + negativeSampleWeight + seed
    -> initialize single-label or multi-label feature plane
    -> create extended batches:
         original batch nodes
       + positive neighbor samples
       + negative samples
    -> expand subgraphs per layer using sample-size fanout
    -> build forward computation graph
    -> build loss graph
    -> backward pass gradients
    -> Adam optimizer updates
    -> model catalog artifact
    -> optional model disk artifact

inference:
  graph + trained model + batchSize + concurrency
    -> validate model compatibility against graph schema and weight properties
    -> initialize feature plane from train config
    -> partition nodes by batchSize
    -> expand subgraphs per layer
    -> forward computation graph
    -> normalize rows
    -> resultFeatures[nodeCount][embeddingDimension]
    -> stream/write/mutate dense vectors
```

The important memory and correctness lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Model weights | `GraphSageTrainEstimateDefinition` prices each layer's weights; POOL adds self weights, neighbor weights, and bias. | Model body should be a durable artifact with a hash, dimensions, aggregator type, and bytes. |
| Multi-label weights | Multi-label training adds `weightsByLabel` ranges based on feature dimension, property count, and label count. | Multi-label mode needs separate admission; it is not just "more features." |
| Initial feature plane | Train/inference both create `HugeObjectArray<double[]>` feature vectors; multi-label uses label-specific feature widths and bias. | Feature storage is a first-class lane and must record label, property, and projected-dimension shape. |
| Extended batches | Training creates batch nodes plus positive neighbors plus negative samples. | Configured `batchSize` understates training memory; receipts should show original and extended batch counts. |
| Sampled subgraphs | `GraphSageHelper.embeddingsEstimation` expands batch node counts by `sampleSize + 1` per layer, clamped by node count. | The cap is controlled by fanout, not only by graph size. Sample sizes are memory knobs. |
| Forward matrices | Inference and training build aggregator computation graphs and normalize rows. | Forward state should be profiled separately from feature/output state. |
| Backward matrices | Training adds backward aggregators and gradients. | Training cannot share the same budget as inference. |
| Adam optimizer | Train estimation prices initial and update optimizer state. | Optimizer state is resident/temporary training overhead that must be shown explicitly. |
| MEAN aggregator | Mean estimator prices one input-dimension buffer plus two embedding-dimension buffers per node. | MEAN should be the lower-RAM compatible training profile. |
| POOL aggregator | Pool estimator prices three previous-node embedding buffers plus six current-node embedding buffers. | POOL should be labeled higher-RAM/higher-capacity, not a hidden config string. |
| Result features | Inference result is `HugeObjectArray<double[]>`; mutate mode makes it resident, non-mutate counts it temporary. | Public mode changes residency. The same algorithm has different cap semantics. |
| Model catalog/disk | Train stores the model in catalog and can persist it to disk. | Model lifecycle receipts must cover train, store, load, validate, infer, and drop. |
| Public rows | Stream maps internal ids to original ids and returns dense embedding lists; write/mutate report side-effect metadata. | Row materialization should stay separate from durable matrix storage. |

The cleanest product profiles are:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible train | Resident model weights, feature plane, sampled subgraphs, forward/backward state, optimizer state, and dense output where requested. | Baseline parity first; highest training peak. | Use for correctness and estimate parity. |
| MEAN low-memory train | Same train semantics, but aggregator constrained to MEAN and small sample sizes/batch size. | Slower convergence or lower expressiveness possible; lower per-batch buffers. | First exact-compatible GraphSAGE training lane if we ever build it. |
| POOL high-capacity train | POOL aggregator with extra weights and larger aggregation buffers. | Higher RAM and likely slower per batch. | A later profile for users who accept higher cost. |
| Batch-capped exact train | Bound batch size and sample sizes, disable eager task caching, and keep only a small number of batch tasks live. | Slower wall time, more scheduling overhead, exact if seed/order semantics match fixtures. | "Fit under 5 GB even if it takes longer" for GNN training. |
| Lazy-task train | Prefer lazy `BatchTask` creation over eager task caching when the cap is tight. | Saves memory at the cost of repeated task construction. | A concrete RAM-for-CPU tradeoff. |
| Feature-plane sidecar | Store feature vectors in mmap/direct pages and decode by batch. | Slower feature access; lower heap pressure. | Useful when feature arrays dominate heap. |
| Model-artifact-first | Persist model weights and train metadata as a compact artifact; keep inference separate. | Adds lifecycle overhead but improves reproducibility. | Makes GraphSAGE more like a model product than one Cypher call. |
| Inference stream-window | Keep result matrix as sidecar or bounded pages; stream original-id rows in windows. | Lower peak row materialization; consumer can dominate wall time. | Safe public API behavior for large embeddings. |
| Mutate resident | Materialize resultFeatures into graph-store residency. | Higher RAM, fastest later reads from graph store. | Explicitly chosen mode, not default magic. |
| Quantized/approximate model | Quantize feature planes, model weights, or output embeddings with tolerance/quality receipts. | Can be lower RAM and faster, but not exact GDS parity by default. | Separate approximate SKU; never hide this under compatibility. |
