Rubber duck check:

```text
Can GraphSAGE use much less RAM than a naive implementation?
  Yes. A naive implementation could accidentally keep feature rows, sampled
  subgraphs, forward matrices, backward matrices, gradients, optimizer state,
  result rows, and model artifacts all resident at once. GDS already separates
  many of these lanes in its estimator, and Knight Bus should copy that discipline.

Can it use much less RAM than GDS?
  Sometimes, but the credible levers are specific: smaller/capped batches,
  lower sample sizes, lazy task creation, sidecar feature planes, sidecar output
  matrices, streamed rows, and explicit approximate compression. These levers
  mostly trade RAM for time or quality.

Will it be faster?
  Resident exact inference can be competitive if vector layout, batch execution,
  row materialization, and feature access improve. Bounded exact training is
  likely slower than a resident path because it reduces live state by doing more
  scheduling, paging, or decoding. Approximate/quantized profiles can be faster,
  but only as explicit non-parity modes.

What is the semantic trap?
  Train and inference are different products. The trained model carries config
  and graph-schema constraints into inference. Sample sizes multiply batch state.
  Extended training batches are roughly 3x original batch size. Multi-label mode
  changes feature shape. POOL is not MEAN with a different label; it has more
  weights and heavier aggregator buffers. Mutate result features are resident,
  while stream/write result features can be temporary or sidecar-backed.

What should the product say?
  "GraphSAGE is a model-and-batch budget. We show model weights, feature plane,
  sampled subgraphs, forward/backward state, optimizer state, result matrix, and
  public materialization separately. Choose exact resident, exact capped, sidecar,
  or approximate mode before the run."
```

#### HashGNN Is The Sparse-To-Dense Proof Precedent

Pass 145 deepens HashGNN because it is the cleanest GDS source precedent for
the Knight Bus storage thesis. GraphSAGE proves that "embedding" can mean model
artifact plus batch graph plus optimizer. FastRP proves that dense embeddings
are often several matrices, not one. HashGNN proves the sharper storage point:
the algorithm can run over compact binary bitsets, while public API output can
still require dense `double[]` materialization. The memory estimator already
names that sparse-to-dense range.

The core shape is:

```text
graph
  + featureProperties OR generateFeatures OR binarizeFeatures
  + iterations
  + embeddingDensity
  + neighborInfluence
  + heterogeneous
  + optional outputDimension
  -> construct input bitset embeddings B
  -> allocate empty bitset embeddings A
  -> for each iteration:
       clear current cache
       precompute hash arrays per density lane and relationship type
       minhash self and neighbor bitsets into current cache
       update active-feature density
       ping-pong A/B
  -> if outputDimension is present:
       projectionMatrix[binaryDimension][outputDimension]
       dense output matrix[nodeCount][outputDimension]
       DoubleArrayNodePropertyValues
     else:
       BinaryArrayNodePropertyValues over the final bitset cache
  -> stream/mutate public output
```

The important memory and correctness lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Binary dimension | `HashGNNMemoryEstimateDefinition` chooses generated-feature dimension, binarized-feature dimension, or 1024 fallback. | Admission must record where the binary dimension came from; this changes both bitset and dense bounds. |
| Embeddings cache 1 and 2 | The estimator prices two per-node `HugeAtomicBitSet` object arrays. Runtime uses A/B ping-pong caches. | The compact core has two live bitset stores, not one. Any profile must show both. |
| Hashes cache | `HashTask.Hashes.memoryEstimation` prices neighbor, self, and pre-aggregation hash arrays; heterogeneous mode multiplies by relationship-type count. | Heterogeneous graphs need a separate hash-state receipt. |
| Generated features | `GenerateFeaturesTask` seeds generated bitsets from original node id and configured density. | Generated features can be recompute-friendly, but deterministic original-id seeding must be preserved. |
| Binarized features | `BinarizeTask` projects numeric features through random property embeddings and thresholding. | Binarization has its own projection matrix, threshold, and scalar-product stats. |
| Raw binary features | `RawFeaturesTask` accepts only binary 0/1 feature values unless binarization is configured. | Compatibility must reject non-binary raw values; it cannot silently coerce. |
| Minhash propagation | `MinHashTask` hashes self and neighbor bitsets, chooses arg-min values, and sets current bits. | Correctness needs hash-triple and arg-min fixtures, not just output-vector snapshots. |
| Heterogeneous graph list | Runtime splits relationship-type-filtered graphs when heterogeneous mode is enabled. | Relationship-type count is a memory and runtime lane. |
| Densify projection matrix | `DensifyTask` builds a `float[binaryDimension][denseDimension]` projection matrix. | Dense output has a materializer cost beyond the final dense matrix. |
| Dense output matrix | Densify allocates `HugeObjectArray<double[]>` and fills dense vectors from set bits. | Dense output should be optional, windowed, or sidecar-backed under tight caps. |
| Binary node-property carrier | `EmbeddingsToNodePropertyValues.fromBinary` wraps binary embeddings and dimension. | The compact artifact can remain binary if the user does not demand dense vectors immediately. |
| Stream rows | Stream builder maps internal ids to original ids and calls `doubleArrayValue`. | Stream mode can force row-level dense conversion even when the algorithm core is sparse. |
| Mutate side effect | Mutate step passes `NodePropertyValues` into graph-store mutation and reports written-property count. | Mutate mode changes residency and must be priced separately from compute. |

The cleanest product profiles are:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible sparse HashGNN | Two bitset caches, hash cache, sparse output carrier when output dimension is absent, public conversion as needed. | Baseline compatibility first; stream/mutate materialization can dominate output time. | First exact parity profile after estimate/config fixtures. |
| Dense-output HashGNN | Sparse propagation plus projection matrix plus dense output matrix. | More memory and densify time; faster downstream dense consumers after materialization. | Use when user explicitly asks for dense embeddings. |
| Binary-artifact-first | Persist final bitset embeddings as the primary artifact and delay dense output. | Fast lower-peak compute; later consumers pay conversion. | Strongest "fit under cap" exact profile if API can tolerate deferred materialization. |
| Output-window densify | Keep bitset result resident or sidecar-backed and densify rows in windows. | Lower peak, more repeated projection/scan work. | "I can spend more time but peak RAM must stay under 5-10 GB." |
| Projection sidecar/recompute | Store or recompute projection matrix under a named seed and dimension. | Recompute saves memory but costs CPU; storing saves CPU but costs RAM/disk. | A visible RAM-vs-latency knob. |
| Generated-feature recompute | Recreate generated feature bitsets from original node id and seed instead of storing them eagerly. | Saves feature-plane memory, costs repeated generation. | Good for generated-feature workloads where feature access is deterministic. |
| Binarize-threshold tuned | Keep property projection and threshold stats as a sidecar. | Adds preprocessing, but shrinks runtime state to bitsets. | Good when raw feature vectors are numeric but sparse binary propagation is desired. |
| Heterogeneous rel-type profile | Keep per-relationship-type filtered graph/hash state explicit. | More hash arrays and graph scans; better semantic fidelity. | Use when relationship-type-specific propagation matters. |
| Strict raw-binary validation | Reject non-0/1 raw values and require binarization for numeric features. | No hidden preprocessing; clearer errors. | Compatibility and trust profile. |
| Approximate compact-only | Return binary or quantized embeddings and skip dense parity by design. | Lowest memory; not exact GDS output parity. | Separate approximate SKU with quality metrics, never hidden under compatibility. |

Rubber duck check:

```text
Can HashGNN use much less RAM than a naive implementation?
  Yes. A naive implementation could accidentally inflate every intermediate
  embedding into dense vectors. GDS's own implementation keeps propagation as
  bitsets and only densifies when outputDimension asks for it.

Can it use much less RAM than GDS?
  Maybe, but the honest answer is profile-specific. GDS already uses compact
  bitsets for the core. Knight Bus can still win by delaying dense output,
  windowing densify, sidecar-backing the final bitset artifact, recomputing
  generated features, or making the projection matrix a seed-backed sidecar.
  Those are concrete RAM-for-time trades, not free wins.

Will it be faster?
  Sparse propagation can be fast because bitsets and minhash arrays are compact.
  Dense materialization can dominate when users ask for stream rows or mutate
  output. A resident dense-output profile may be faster for downstream consumers
  after it pays the upfront densify cost. A bounded/windowed profile is likely
  slower but more predictable.

What is the semantic trap?
  The estimate fixture says relationship count, concurrency, and iterations do
  not change the memory estimate in the inspected matrix, but runtime still
  scans relationships and loops over iterations. Generated features use original
  node ids for deterministic seeds. Raw mode accepts only 0/1 values. Setting
  outputDimension changes the carrier and estimate from sparse range to fixed
  dense output. Heterogeneous mode multiplies relationship-type hash state.

What should the product say?
  "HashGNN is a sparse-to-dense storage contract. We run the algorithm over
  bitsets, show the two caches and hash arrays, then let you choose binary
  artifact, dense output, windowed densify, or approximate compact mode before
  the run."
```

#### GDS Estimate Admission Is The Product Spine

Pass 146 is not about one more algorithm. It is about the product contract that
all algorithm-specific storage profiles must plug into. The strongest current
thesis is:

```text
algorithm-specific storage reduces peak RAM only when the product can:
  1. estimate the graph-load bytes,
  2. estimate the algorithm bytes,
  3. explain the min/max range as a tree,
  4. select a bound policy before execution,
  5. reserve or reject before compute,
  6. record actual phase timings and peak usage after compute.
```

GDS already gives us the shape of this product spine. `AlgorithmEstimationTemplate`
accepts a graph name or a projection map, computes graph dimensions, optionally
adds graph-load memory, attaches an algorithm estimate, and returns a
`MemoryEstimateResult`. `MemoryEstimateResult` is not just a string. It is a
public row with `requiredMemory`, `treeView`, `mapView`, `bytesMin`, `bytesMax`,
`nodeCount`, `relationshipCount`, and heap percentages. `MemoryTree` keeps the
component structure explainable. `MemoryRange` keeps min and max as first-class
values. The validators and algorithm guard then turn the estimate into an
admission decision before work runs.

The core flow to mirror is:

```text
estimate request
  graphName OR graph projection map
  + algorithm config
  + memoryEstimation
  + optional dimension transformer
  -> graph dimensions
  -> optional graph loading estimate
  -> algorithm memory tree
  -> MemoryEstimateResult
       requiredMemory
       treeView
       mapView
       bytesMin / bytesMax
       nodeCount / relationshipCount
       heapPercentageMin / heapPercentageMax

execution request
  load and validate graph
  -> MemoryRequirement selects min or max by policy
  -> MemoryTracker reserves bytes, or sudo tracks without checking
  -> compute with metrics
  -> process side effect
  -> render result
```

That gives Knight Bus a clean layered design:

```text
        User cap: 5 GB / 10 GB / 50 GB / no cap
                         |
                         v
      +----------------------------------------+
      | Estimate endpoint                       |
      | graph bytes + algorithm bytes + output  |
      +----------------------------------------+
                         |
                         v
      +----------------------------------------+
      | Bound policy                            |
      | max-strict | min-risk | selected-profile|
      +----------------------------------------+
                         |
                         v
      +----------------------------------------+
      | Admission guard                         |
      | reserve | reject | sudo-with-audit      |
      +----------------------------------------+
                         |
                         v
      +----------------------------------------+
      | Algorithm-specific storage profile      |
      | CSR, frontier, queue, bitset, sidecar    |
      +----------------------------------------+
                         |
                         v
      +----------------------------------------+
      | Execution receipt                       |
      | load, compute, side effect, render, RSS |
      +----------------------------------------+
```

The important lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Graph input mode | `AlgorithmEstimationTemplate` accepts graph name or map. `MemoryEstimationGraphConfigParser` validates projection/query inputs. | Support actual named graph estimates and fictitious "what if" estimates. Reject ambiguous maps before making a RAM promise. |
| Graph-load estimate | `DatabaseGraphStoreEstimationService` and `FictitiousGraphStoreEstimationService` produce graph dimensions and graph-load bytes. | Keep graph storage bytes separate from algorithm bytes, because custom OLAP formats may change either independently. |
| Algorithm estimate | The shared template adds an algorithm memory tree under an `algorithm` component. | Every algorithm profile must expose its own estimator before compute exists. |
| Recursive memory tree | `MemoryTree.render` and `renderMap` expose nested component structure. | Receipts should show why a profile fits or fails, not only one final number. |
| Min/max range | `MemoryRange` is algebraic and validates range sanity. | Preserve uncertainty as a range; do not collapse to a fake exact number. |
| Bound policy | `MemoryUsageValidator` and `MemoryRequirement` select min or max based on policy. | Default budget-bounded mode should use selected-profile max. Min-bound mode can exist only with a visible risk label. |
| Builder lanes | `MemoryEstimations` gives per-node, per-thread, per-dimension, and max/high-water components. | Build a small Rust estimator DSL: fixed, per node, per relationship, per thread, per feature, per output row, per frontier, max live branch. |
| Sudo override | GDS sudo bypasses validation but still tracks bytes. | Expose override as an audited power-user path, never as the default. |
| Algorithm memory guard | `ComputationService` guards before `computeWithMetrics`. | Strict bounded mode must reject when an estimate is missing. GDS may skip; Knight Bus should not when the product promise is a cap. |
| Processing phases | `DefaultAlgorithmProcessingTemplate` separates load/validate, compute, side effect, and render. | Report phase timings and phase memory deltas so latency/RAM tradeoffs are visible. |
| Local foothold | `project_estimate_row_now` already emits the core graph-project estimate columns. | Extend the local estimate row into algorithm-profile estimates instead of inventing a disconnected API. |

The product profiles that fall out:

| Profile | Policy | What User Learns |
|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible estimate row | Match GDS columns first. | "This rewrite speaks the same estimate language." |
| Cap-strict max-bound | Compare cap against selected-profile max. | "If we say it fits, we reserve against the conservative bound." |
| Optimistic min-bound | Compare cap against min with warning. | "This may fit, but the high-water branch can exceed your cap." |
| Selected-profile bound | Compute min/max for a specific storage profile. | "Queue-only, graph-materialized, sidecar, and windowed modes have different RAM curves." |
| Dry-run fictitious graph | Estimate from counts and projection config. | "Here is what a 50 GB source dataset probably costs before you ingest it." |
| Actual graph catalog estimate | Estimate from a named graph. | "Here is what the already-loaded graph plus algorithm will cost." |
| Sudo override with audit | Track bytes but do not block. | "You bypassed the guard and accepted the risk." |
| Estimate-missing reject | Bounded mode refuses unpriced algorithms. | "No estimate, no bounded-RAM promise." |
| Phase receipt | Return load, compute, side-effect, render, and peak RSS. | "The planner was either right or wrong in a measurable way." |


Rubber duck check:

```text
Is this the innovative part?
  Not by itself. GDS already has much of the estimate/admission machinery.
  The innovation is making it the explicit product shell around many custom
  storage profiles, then proving each profile with receipts and benchmarks.

Does this reduce RAM?
  No. The estimate/admission spine does not reduce RAM. It makes RAM reduction
  enforceable, visible, selectable, and falsifiable.

Can we say Neo4j always blocks on the maximum estimate?
  No. The inspected setting `gds.validate_using_max_memory_estimation` defaults
  false, so GDS can validate against the minimum estimate unless configured
  otherwise. Knight Bus should be explicit about our stricter default.

What is the strongest product sentence?
  "Before we run, we show graph bytes, algorithm bytes, output bytes, selected
  bound, and selected storage profile. Then we reserve against that bound and
  return a receipt showing whether reality matched the estimate."

What should happen in bounded mode if an estimate is missing?
  Reject. GDS can skip the guard for missing estimates, but Knight Bus cannot
  call itself budget-bounded if unpriced work is allowed through the gate.
```

#### Pregel Runtime Progress Turns Admission Into A Running Contract

Pass 147 deepens the layer after estimate/admission. Pass 146 answered:

```text
Can this job fit under the user's cap before we start?
```

Pregel answers the next question:

```text
Once admitted, can this iterative job run visibly, cancel safely, converge
explainably, and materialize only the output mode the user asked for?
```

This matters because PageRank-like algorithms are not just "scan graph and
return vector." In GDS, they are runtime state machines:

```text
Pregel.create
  -> validate config concurrency
  -> validate inverse indexes for bidirectional computations
  -> allocate NodeValue from computation schema
  -> choose messenger:
       reducer present -> ReducingMessenger
       no reducer + async -> AsyncQueueMessenger
       no reducer + sync -> SyncQueueMessenger
  -> choose computer:
       partitioning AUTO -> ForkJoinComputer
       otherwise -> PartitionedComputer
  -> allocate vote bits
  -> attach ProgressTracker

Pregel.run
  -> init computation
  -> for iteration in 0..maxIterations:
       assert termination flag
       begin "Compute iteration"
       init compute step
       init messenger
       run compute step
       end "Compute iteration"
       begin "Master compute iteration"
       run masterCompute
       check master convergence OR no messages + all vote bits set
       end "Master compute iteration"
       break if converged
  -> return nodeValues, didConverge, ranIterations
  -> release computer state in finally
```

The most important thing this pass adds to the PMF thesis is that "bounded RAM"
is also a **runtime profile** problem:

```text
estimate profile:
  predicts bytes

admission profile:
  decides accept/refuse/override

runtime profile:
  chooses messenger, scheduler, partitioning, task creation, and cancellation

output profile:
  chooses stream/stats/mutate/write materialization

receipt:
  proves what actually happened
```

The key runtime lanes are:

| Lane | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Receipt Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Node-value schema | `BasePregelComputation.schema` defines named public/private node values. `NodeValue.memoryEstimation` prices LONG, DOUBLE, LONG_ARRAY, and DOUBLE_ARRAY differently. | Record schema keys, visibility, value type, backing array type, bytes, and whether output exposes the value. |
| Reducer mode | `BasePregelComputation.reducer` can combine messages to a node, and the comment says it can significantly reduce memory and runtime. | Expose reducing messenger as a profile only when algebra permits it; never silently substitute it. |
| Sync queue mode | `SyncQueueMessenger` swaps current/previous queues each iteration. Sync queue estimate includes current queues, previous queues, tails, and reference counts. | Record two-queue memory and swap policy. |
| Async queue mode | `AsyncQueueMessenger` compacts queues after iteration 0. Async queue estimate includes queues, heads, tails, and reference counts. | Record compaction policy and async semantics separately from sync. |
| Reducing message arrays | `ReducingMessenger` keeps send/receive atomic-double arrays and optional sender arrays. | Record send/receive bytes, reducer identity, and sender tracking bytes. |
| Vote bits | `Pregel.memoryEstimation` adds one per-node `HugeAtomicBitSet`. | Convergence memory is a named O(V) lane. |
| Compute steps | `Pregel.memoryEstimation` adds per-thread `PartitionedComputeStep` overhead. | Concurrency affects more than scheduling; it has an estimate lane. |
| Partitioned executor | `PartitionedComputer` uses range or degree partitions and a shared executor through `RunWithConcurrency`. | Record partition strategy, task count, graph-copy count, and executor ownership. |
| Fork-join executor | `ForkJoinComputer` owns a fork-join pool and `ForkJoinComputeStep` recursively splits until 1000 nodes. | Record fork threshold, recursive split high-water, and pool lifecycle. |
| Active-node rule | `ComputeStep.computeBatch` computes only if a node has messages or has not voted to halt. | Record active-node counts by iteration and why work was skipped. |
| Progress tree | `Pregel.progressTask` creates a dynamic iterative task with compute and master-compute leaves. | Record task tree, dynamic iteration mode, canceled pending leaves, and current iteration. |
| Termination flag | `Pregel.run` and `RunWithConcurrency` check termination before work and while scheduling/waiting. | Receipt should distinguish converged, maxIterations, canceled, interrupted, failed, and refused. |
| Lazy scheduling | `RunWithConcurrency` advances lazy task iterators at most one item ahead and caps running tasks by concurrency. | Do not precreate huge task lists; record task-created high-water. |
| Output materialization | Pregel stream walks all nodes/public schema, stats emits iterations/convergence/timings/config, mutate writes public node properties. | Compute bytes and output bytes must be separate. |

The numeric fixture evidence is especially useful:

| Scenario | GDS Fixture Bytes At 10k Nodes / 100k Relationships |
|---|---:|
| Queue-based sync, one LONG property, concurrency 1 | 7,441,752 |
| Queue-based sync, one LONG property, concurrency 10 | 7,442,256 |
| Queue-based async, one LONG property, concurrency 1 | 3,841,688 |
| Queue-based async, one LONG property, concurrency 10 | 3,842,192 |
| Reducing message arrays, one LONG property, no sender tracking | 241,584 |
| Reducing message arrays, one LONG property, sender tracking | 401,664 |
| Queue-based sync, LONG + DOUBLE + LONG_ARRAY + DOUBLE_ARRAY, concurrency 1 | 9,441,824 |
| Queue-based async, LONG + DOUBLE + LONG_ARRAY + DOUBLE_ARRAY, concurrency 1 | 5,841,760 |
| Reducing arrays, LONG + DOUBLE + LONG_ARRAY + DOUBLE_ARRAY, concurrency 1 | 2,241,656 |

The point is not "always use reducing arrays." The point is subtler and more
valuable:

```text
message algebra decides storage shape.

If the algorithm has a valid reducer:
  reducing arrays can be dramatically smaller and faster.

If the algorithm needs arbitrary per-node message queues:
  queue mode preserves semantics but costs more.

If the user asks for sender tracking:
  sender arrays are a real memory lane.
```

That suggests these product profiles:

| Profile | RAM Shape | Latency Shape | Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDS-compatible partitioned Pregel | Node values, vote bits, selected messenger, partitioned compute steps, shared executor. | Predictable baseline; good first parity target. | "Same runtime semantics, visible receipt." |
| Reducing-messenger Pregel | Two per-node atomic arrays plus optional sender arrays. | Often faster/lower RAM when reducer semantics fit. | "Use algebra to shrink message state." |
| Sync-queue Pregel | Current/previous queues plus tails/reference counts. | Stronger superstep separation; higher resident queue memory. | "Compatibility for queue-shaped messages." |
| Async-queue Pregel | One queue family with compaction. | Lower estimate than sync in fixture; semantics differ. | "Async profile when algorithm/config allows it." |
| Fork-join auto Pregel | Recursive tasks, fork-join pool, 1000-node split threshold. | Can improve scheduling on skewed work, but profile is less static. | "Latency profile, not first strict-memory profile." |
| Lazy bounded scheduler | Create tasks as needed, run at most concurrency cap, cancel outstanding tasks on abort. | Slight scheduling overhead, better memory predictability. | "Do not preallocate all work just to parallelize." |
| Phase-released Pregel | Release messenger/vote/compute-step state once final node values are stable. | Same compute, lower post-compute residency before output. | "Make output materialization the next separate decision." |
| Stream-window Pregel output | Keep node values resident or sidecar-backed, stream public rows in windows. | Lower output peak, slower all-row materialization. | "Fit under cap when user accepts more render time." |

The minimal Pregel runtime receipt should look like:

```yaml
runtime:
  algorithm: gds.pageRank.stream
  graphName: optional
  nodeCount: integer
  relationshipCount: integer
  maxIterations: integer
  ranIterations: integer
  didConverge: boolean
  convergenceReason: masterCompute | noMessagesAndAllVotes | maxIterations | canceled | failed
  terminationChecks: integer

config:
  partitioning: RANGE | DEGREE | AUTO
  useForkJoin: boolean
  concurrency: integer
  isAsynchronous: boolean
  hasReducer: boolean
  trackSender: boolean

state:
  nodeValues:
    - key: string
      type: LONG | DOUBLE | LONG_ARRAY | DOUBLE_ARRAY
      visibility: PUBLIC | PRIVATE
      estimatedBytes: integer
  voteBitsBytes: integer
  computeStepBytes: integer

messenger:
  mode: reducing | syncQueue | asyncQueue
  reducerIdentity: optional
  senderTracking: boolean
  queueBytes: integer
  sendArrayBytes: integer
  receiveArrayBytes: integer
  resetPolicy: swap | compact | reduceIdentityFill
  releaseIteration: postCompute

scheduler:
  mode: sequential | boundedExecutor | forkJoin
  partitionsCreated: integer
  tasksCreatedHighWater: integer
  tasksRunningHighWater: integer
  iteratorLookahead: integer
  forkSequentialThreshold: optional
  waitPolicy: optional
  mayInterruptIfRunning: boolean

progress:
  taskTree: object
  currentIteration: integer
  computeProgressUnits: integer
  masterProgressUnits: integer
  canceledPendingIterationLeaves: integer
  failedTask: optional

output:
  mode: stream | stats | mutate | write
  publicSchemaKeys: array
  originalIdMapping: boolean
  rowsMaterialized: integer
  nodePropertiesWritten: optional
  materializationBytes: integer
  materializationMillis: integer
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
Does this pass change the first implementation recommendation?
  No. WCC remains the first exact starter slice because it is simpler. Pregel is
  the PageRank prerequisite and the first serious iterative-runtime proof.

Does Pregel prove a massive RAM win over GDS?
  No. It proves where RAM lives. Some choices, especially reducing messenger
  versus queue messenger, can be huge, but only when algorithm semantics allow
  that choice.

Is fork-join automatically better?
  Not for strict RAM. Fork-join is a scheduling/latency profile. It can be good,
  but recursive task splitting and pool ownership need receipts before claims.

What is the trap?
  Treating progress logs as cosmetic. In a budget-bounded batch product,
  progress state is part of the contract because users need to know whether a
  job converged, canceled pending iterations, hit maxIterations, failed, or was
  externally terminated.

What should the product say?
  "After admission, we run with a named runtime profile. The receipt shows the
  messenger, scheduler, task tree, iterations, convergence reason, release
  points, and output materialization cost."
```

#### Job Progress Observability Makes Bounded Compute Product-Grade

Pass 148 deepens the operational layer around the algorithm. The important
question is no longer only:

```text
Can this job fit?
```

or:

```text
Which runtime/storage profile did it use?
```

It is:

```text
While this bounded batch graph job is running, can the user see it, trust it,
cancel it, inspect warnings, and understand whether cleanup happened?
```

The answer in Neo4j GDS is a small but meaningful lifecycle plane:

```text
procedure call
  -> create or receive JobId
  -> create request-scoped TaskRegistry for database + user
  -> register base Task in per-database TaskStore
  -> attach memory footprint and requested concurrency to the task
  -> run nested subtasks through TaskProgressTracker
  -> emit progress rows via gds.listProgress(jobId)
  -> attach warning messages to UserLog
  -> check TerminationFlag separately from algorithm convergence
  -> unregister task and release progress logger on completion/failure
```

That seems like plumbing until you view it through the Knight Bus thesis. A
strict-RAM graph product is asking users to trust a contract:

```text
I will run this expensive graph job under a declared budget and tell you why
the result is correct.
```

For that promise, the job table is not cosmetic. It is the user's live audit
window.

| Surface | GDS Evidence | Knight Bus Product Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Public progress procedure | `ListProgressProc` exposes `gds.listProgress(jobId)`. | Long-running graph jobs need a queryable control-plane surface. |
| User/admin scope | `OperationsApplications.listProgress` lets admins query by job id across users, while normal users query their own tasks. | The job plane needs permissions from day one if it is multi-user. |
| Addressable task state | `TaskStore` supports queries by all tasks, job id, username, and username plus job id. | A run receipt should be addressable by database, user, job id, and task id. |
| Shared database store | `PerDatabaseTaskStore` stores username -> job id -> user task in concurrent maps. | Graph jobs are database-scoped product objects, not local variables. |
| Per-request registry | `TaskRegistryFactoryService` documents shared database stores plus per-request registries. | A new request should get clean registration while still writing into shared observable state. |
| Task tree rows | `DefaultResultRenderer` walks a task tree with `JobProgressVisitor` and emits `ProgressResult`. | A receipt should expose a phase tree, not just one percentage number. |
| Memory/concurrency in progress | `Task` carries estimated memory range and max concurrency; `TaskProgressTracker` sets them. | The live progress surface should show the exact budget and parallelism profile being exercised. |
| Warnings | `TaskProgressTracker.logMessage(WARNING, ...)` writes user-log entries. | Spill, cap fallback, approximation caveats, and skipped side effects must be visible. |
| Termination | `TerminationFlag` and `TerminationFlagImpl` are separate from task finish and convergence. | Converged, canceled, terminated, failed, and refused are different outcomes. |
| Cleanup | `TaskProgressTracker.release` unregisters task and releases the progress logger. | Stale running jobs are a trust failure, so release is a tested lifecycle event. |

The core design implication is:

```text
bounded compute = estimate plane + admission plane + runtime plane
                + job observability plane + output/receipt plane
```

Without the observability plane, the product can still benchmark well, but it
will feel like an opaque batch script. With it, the user can ask:

```text
What is running?
Who owns it?
Which graph and algorithm is it using?
Which storage profile was selected?
What memory range was promised?
What concurrency was requested?
Which phase is active?
How far along is it?
Did we spill, cap, approximate, or downgrade anything?
Can I cancel it?
If it stopped, did it converge, fail, terminate, or get refused?
Was task state cleaned up?
```

That suggests a first Knight Bus job-control contract:

```yaml
job:
  jobId: string
  database: string
  username: string
  algorithm: gds.wcc.stream | gds.bfs.stream | gds.pageRank.stream
  graphName: string
  mode: stream | stats | mutate | write
  status: admitted | running | succeeded | failed | canceled | refused

budget:
  capBytes: integer
  boundPolicy: max | min-with-risk | observed-only
  estimatedBytesMin: integer
  estimatedBytesMax: integer
  selectedStorageProfile: string
  requestedConcurrency: integer

progress:
  taskTree:
    - depth: integer
      taskName: string
      status: pending | running | finished | failed | canceled
      progress: string
      progressBar: string
      timeStarted: optional
      elapsedTime: string
      estimatedMemoryRangeBytes: optional
      maxConcurrency: optional

events:
  warnings:
    - taskName: string
      message: string
      timeStarted: string
  termination:
    source: none | user | transaction | deadline | external
    lastCheckMillis: optional
    thrownCause: optional
    finalOutcome: converged | maxIterations | canceled | terminated | failed | refused

cleanup:
  taskRegistered: boolean
  taskUnregistered: boolean
  taskStoreCountAfterRelease: integer
  releaseMillis: integer
```

3. `test_job_progress_list_respects_user_and_admin_scope_now`
4. `test_list_progress_returns_running_task_tree_now`
5. `test_progress_row_schema_matches_gds_columns_now`
6. `test_progress_task_records_memory_range_and_concurrency_now`

10. `test_failed_job_marks_task_failed_and_releases_state_now`
11. `profile_job_task_registry_receipt_v1`
12. `profile_job_progress_row_schema_v1`
13. `profile_task_lifecycle_release_receipt_v1`

Architecture options:

| Option | What It Is | Why It Helps | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal fixture-only job table | In-memory map for local WCC/PageRank/BFS tests. | Fastest route to proving receipt shape. | Not enough for production or multi-process runs. |
| Per-database in-memory task store | GDS-like concurrent database-scoped store. | Good compatibility with `gds.listProgress` mental model. | Loses history across process restart unless paired with durable receipts. |
| Append-only job event log | Every phase/warning/progress/cancel event is appended to durable storage. | Best for proof-carrying runs and postmortems. | Requires compaction/sampling so progress logging does not dominate writes. |
| SQLite-backed job control plane | `jobs`, `job_tasks`, `job_events`, `job_warnings`, `job_receipts`. | Easy to query, sync, and hand to LLM agents. | Must avoid hot-path per-edge writes; event batching is mandatory. |
| Hybrid live map plus durable receipt | In-memory live state for `listProgress`; durable event/receipt at phase boundaries. | Good default for low overhead and trustworthy final artifacts. | Live and durable views must reconcile. |

My recommendation is the hybrid:

```text
hot path:
  in-memory live task tree, updated at phase/progress cadence

durable path:
  append receipt events at admission, phase start/end, warning, termination,
  output materialization, and cleanup

query path:
  gds.listProgress reads live state while running, then final receipt reads the
  durable artifact after completion
```

Why not write every progress tick to SQLite? Because bounded graph algorithms
can update progress frequently, and turning observability into a write-heavy
bottleneck would be self-sabotage. The live map gives quick status. The durable
receipt gives proof.

Current local Knight Bus boundary:

```text
Present:
  Cypher walk cancellation/deadline helpers.
  Bolt metadata mapping for termination state.
  GDS registry and dispatcher shell.
  GDS graph/project estimate row envelope.

Missing:
  GDS job id lifecycle.
  GDS task store.
  GDS listProgress surface.
  GDS task tree rows.
  GDS user warning log.
  GDS algorithm cancellation receipt.
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
Does this pass replace WCC-first implementation?
  No. WCC remains the first algorithm slice. This pass says that once an
  algorithm can run longer than a tiny fixture, it needs a job-control wrapper.

Is listProgress enough by itself?
  No. It is the live query surface. The final product also needs durable
  receipts for estimate, admission, execution, warnings, output, and cleanup.

Should job observability be built before every algorithm?
  Not before tiny fixture parity. But before PageRank/BFS/KNN-style long runs,
  yes, because a RAM-cap product without a live job plane feels opaque.

What is the main product phrase?
  "Bounded graph compute should be watchable while it runs and auditable after
  it finishes."
```

#### Job Progress Test Oracles Turn Observability Into A Gate

Pass 149 turns the pass 148 observability architecture into something more
useful for implementation: a test-oracle list.

The earlier section says Knight Bus needs a job-control plane. This pass says
how we know that plane is real.

Neo4j GDS is useful here because its operational tests do not only check the
happy path. They check the boring-but-decisive boundaries:

```text
empty store does not explode
progress rows have stable fields
job ids are parseable
normal users see their own jobs
admins can query more broadly
duplicate job ids are rejected
remove is idempotent
task stores are per database
registries are per request/user
explicit jobId config reaches the task store
warnings are stored and queryable
success releases live task state
failure releases live task state
Pregel stream/write/mutate failure releases live task state
```

That list is small compared with the algorithm code, but it matters because
the product promise is trust under constraint:

```text
I accepted this job under a declared RAM cap.
I can show you what it is doing while it runs.
I can explain warnings and downgrades.
I can prove that it ended, failed, canceled, or cleaned up correctly.
```

If the control plane fails, the algorithm can be correct and still feel
untrustworthy.

| GDS Test Oracle | What It Proves | Knight Bus Red Test |
|---|---|---|
| `ListProgressProcTest.shouldNotFailWhenTheTaskStoreIsEmpty` | `gds.listProgress()` on an empty store is harmless. | `test_gds_list_progress_empty_store_is_harmless_now` |
| `ListProgressProcTest.canListProgressEvent` | Running tasks render user, task, progress, bar, status, start time, and elapsed time. | `test_gds_list_progress_row_schema_matches_gds_fixture_now` |
| `ListProgressProcTest.shouldReturnValidJobId` | Every listed job id is parseable as a `JobId`. | `test_gds_list_progress_job_id_is_valid_now` |
| `ListProgressProcTest.progressIsListedFilteredByUser` | Users do not see each other's tasks. | `test_gds_list_progress_filters_by_username_now` |
| `PerDatabaseTaskStoreTest.shouldBeIdempotentOnRemove` | Repeated cleanup is safe. | `test_gds_task_store_remove_is_idempotent_now` |
| `PerDatabaseTaskStoreTest.shouldQueryByUser` | User plus job-id query is exact. | `test_gds_task_store_queries_by_user_and_job_id_now` |
| `PerDatabaseTaskStoreTest.shouldCountAcrossUsers` | Store high-water/count logic crosses users without losing isolation. | `test_gds_task_store_counts_across_users_now` |
| `LocalTaskRegistryFactoryTest.shouldThrowOnDuplicateJobId` | Duplicate live job id creation fails. | `test_gds_task_registry_rejects_duplicate_job_id_now` |
| `TaskRegistryTest.shouldDetectAlreadyRegisteredTasks` | Registry identity and contains semantics are observable. | `test_gds_task_registry_contains_registered_task_now` |
| `TaskStoreServiceTest.shouldRespectToggle` | Disabled progress tracking has an explicit empty-store path. | `test_gds_task_store_service_respects_progress_tracking_toggle_now` |
| `TaskStoreServiceTest.shouldGetOrCreatePerDatabase` | Same database reuses one store; different databases do not. | `test_gds_task_store_service_reuses_store_per_database_now` |
| `ProcedureExecutorTest.shouldRegisterTaskWithCorrectJobId` | Configured job id survives into task registration. | `test_gds_job_id_from_request_config_reaches_task_store_listener_now` |
| `AlgorithmCleanupTest.cleanupTaskRegistryUnderRegularExecution` | Success releases live task state. | `test_gds_algorithm_success_releases_task_store_now` |
| `AlgorithmCleanupTest.cleanupTaskRegistryWhenTheAlgorithmFails` | Failure releases live task state. | `test_gds_algorithm_failure_releases_task_store_now` |
| `PregelProcTest` stream/write/mutate failure cleanup tests | Pregel output modes clean up even when compute throws. | `test_gds_pregel_stream_write_mutate_failure_releases_task_store_now` |

| `PerDatabaseUserLogStoreTest` warning fixtures | Warnings are grouped by user and task and remain queryable. | `test_gds_user_log_store_groups_warnings_by_user_and_task_now` |
| `UserLogServicesTest` scoping fixtures | Warning stores are database scoped and registry factories are database plus user scoped. | `test_gds_user_log_service_scopes_by_database_and_user_now` |
| `UserLogProcTest.shouldLogUserWarnings` | Public user-log procedure forwards to the operations facade. | `test_gds_user_log_proc_forwards_warning_stream_now` |

The implementation lesson is to build the job-control plane as a product
spine, not as helper state hanging off WCC/PageRank/BFS:

```text
gds procedure call
  -> parse config and jobId
  -> estimate memory lanes
  -> admit or refuse under cap
  -> register live task
  -> run algorithm phases
  -> emit throttled progress updates
  -> attach warnings
  -> handle cancellation or failure
  -> materialize output
  -> release live task
  -> persist final receipt
```

The minimal compatible schema is:

```yaml
liveTaskStore:
  database: string
  username: string
  jobId: string
  taskName: string
  status: running | failed | canceled | finished
  progress: string
  progressBar: string
  timeStarted: string
  elapsedTime: string
  estimatedBytesMin: integer
  estimatedBytesMax: integer
  requestedConcurrency: integer

warningStore:
  database: string
  username: string
  jobId: string
  taskName: string
  message: string
  timeStarted: string
  sequence: integer

receipt:
  jobId: string
  admissionVerdict: admitted | refused
  selectedProfile: string
  finalOutcome: succeeded | failed | canceled | terminated | refused
  taskStoreCountAfterRelease: integer
  warningsCount: integer
  cleanupVerified: boolean
```

Recommended implementation order:

1. Build fixture-only `GdsJobTaskStore` with empty-query, register, remove,
   duplicate-job-id, query-by-user, query-by-user-job, and count tests.
2. Add `gds.listProgress` row rendering with GDS-compatible fields.
3. Add explicit job-id propagation from config into task registration.
4. Add warning store and `gds.userLog`-like query surface.
5. Wrap WCC fixture execution with register/release on success and failure.
6. Only then use the same wrapper for PageRank/BFS/Pregel-style longer jobs.

Receipt profiles to introduce:

```text
profile_gds_list_progress_fixture_receipt_v1
profile_gds_task_store_query_receipt_v1
profile_gds_task_registry_duplicate_receipt_v1
profile_gds_task_store_service_receipt_v1
profile_gds_task_cleanup_failure_receipt_v1
profile_gds_pregel_cleanup_mode_receipt_v1
profile_gds_jobid_propagation_receipt_v1
profile_gds_user_log_fixture_receipt_v1
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
Could this be deferred until after algorithms?
  For tiny WCC fixture parity, yes. For any serious bounded-memory run, no.
  The whole PMF promise is budgeted work that can be watched and audited.

Is this a storage-format innovation?
  Not directly. It is the trust layer around storage-format innovation.
  Without it, cap fallback and spill behavior become invisible.

Does this replace estimate/admission receipts?
  No. It joins them. The receipt chain is estimate -> admission -> live task
  -> warnings -> execution -> output -> cleanup.

What should future LLM coding agents read first?
  The GDS progress/user-log tests before algorithm internals when implementing
  the control plane, then WCC/PageRank/BFS internals when implementing compute.
```

#### WCC Should Be The First Job-Control Customer

Pass 150 connects two lines of evidence that were previously adjacent but not
fully joined:

```text
job-control plane:
  estimate -> admission -> live progress -> warnings -> cleanup -> receipt

WCC-first algorithm slice:
  registry -> estimate -> topology adapter -> DSS union -> stream/stats output
```

The combined thesis is:

```text
Do not implement WCC as an isolated function.
Implement WCC as the first boring, exact, proof-carrying GDS job.
```

Why WCC first?

1. It is small enough to make exact.
2. It exercises real graph topology, not only catalog metadata.
3. It has clear GDS stream and stats oracles.
4. Its memory model is easy to explain: mostly disjoint-set state.
5. It gives the job-control plane something real to wrap.
6. It keeps PageRank/BFS/KNN from becoming the first place we debug job state.

The first supported WCC slice should be deliberately narrow:

| Surface | First Status | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `gds.wcc.stream.estimate` | Support first or same pass as stream | The budget loop must exist before compute. |
| `gds.wcc.stats.estimate` | Support first or same pass as stats | Same estimate shell, same DSS memory lane. |
| `gds.wcc.stream` | Support first runtime mode | Small public output: `nodeId`, `componentId`. |
| `gds.wcc.stats` | Support alongside or immediately after stream | Aggregates the same computation into count/distribution/timings/config. |
| `gds.wcc.write` | Keep registered unsupported | Database write-back is a side-effect contract, not needed for first OLAP proof. |
| `gds.wcc.mutate` | Keep registered unsupported | Graph-catalog mutation needs invalidation/rollback receipts. |
| Seeded WCC | Defer | Seed state changes DSS initialization and roughly doubles the large-node memory lane. |
| Threshold WCC | Defer | Requires relationship-weight lookup, missing-weight fallback, and strict `>` predicate tests. |
| Sampled/undirected/inverse-indexed WCC | Defer or explicitly scope | GDS chooses sampled strategy for undirected or inverse-indexed graphs. |

The first runtime scope should be:

```text
mode:
  stream + stats

graph:
  named projected fixture graph with explicit endpoint topology

orientation:
  NATURAL only, unless the adapter has explicit reverse/undirected receipts

weights:
  unweighted only

seed:
  none

component ids:
  verify by equivalence classes, not literal ids, unless a seeded/consecutive-id
  test is in scope

job control:
  register task, expose live row, release task on success/failure, persist
  final receipt
```

The GDS tests make the first output contract very concrete:

| Oracle | What We Should Port |
|---|---|
| `WccStreamProcTest.testStreamWithDefaults` | Ten-node graph produces three component partitions. |
| `WccStreamProcTest.communitySizeInputs` | `minComponentSize: 1` emits all ten nodes; `minComponentSize: 3` emits only the seven-node component. |
| `WccStatsProcTest.yields` | Stats row has `componentCount = 3`, distribution min/max/mean/percentiles, nonnegative timings, and default config. |
| `WccStatsProcTest.zeroComponentsInEmptyGraph` | Empty projected graph stats returns `componentCount = 0`. |
| `WccStatsProcTest.statsShouldNotHaveWriteProperties` | Stats mode must not leak write columns or write config. |
| `WccTest.shouldComputeComponents` | Algorithm-level tests should assert component regions across orientation inputs. |

The first Knight Bus red-test ladder should be:

1. `test_wcc_inventory_contains_eight_public_rows_now`
2. `test_wcc_stream_and_stats_estimate_links_are_consistent_now`
3. `test_wcc_write_mutate_remain_registered_unsupported_now`
4. `test_wcc_dispatch_status_and_registry_agree_now`
5. `test_gds_job_progress_empty_store_is_harmless_now`
6. `test_gds_job_id_from_request_config_reaches_task_store_listener_now`
7. `test_wcc_estimate_columns_match_gds_shell_now`
8. `test_wcc_estimate_does_not_mutate_catalog_now`

The implementation spine:

```text

  -> exact WCC TSV rows and estimate links

request gate
  -> graph name plus algorithm config, not property-stream fields

estimate gate
  -> GDS-compatible estimate columns, DSS lane in map/tree view

  -> explicit endpoint iterator or typed topology-missing refusal

job gate

compute gate
  -> unsampled unweighted union over endpoint rows

  -> stream rows and stats rows with no default receipt-column drift

  -> sidecar/final receipt with memory lanes, strategy scope, partitions,
     timings, cleanup verdict, and unsupported sibling modes
```

Rubber duck check:

```text
Could we implement WCC faster without job-control?
  Yes, but it would undercut the main product thesis. We are not building a
  graph algorithm toy; we are building budget-bounded graph jobs.

Why not start with PageRank?
  PageRank is more differentiated for iterative-state storage, but it pulls in
  Pregel runtime, convergence, message state, and score tolerances. WCC is the
  better first proof of the shell.

Why not implement write/mutate immediately?
  The thesis is custom OLAP under bounded RAM. Write/mutate introduce side
  effects and invalidation. They should stay registered unsupported until their
  receipts exist.

What does success look like?
  A user can run WCC stream/stats under a declared cap, watch the job, get exact
  GDS-compatible rows, inspect a receipt, and see cleanup verified.
```

#### DAHA And SANCUS Turn Planning Into A Runtime Contract

DAHA and SANCUS add the next layer above "storage format." They say the physical
profile is not finished when the data layout is chosen. It also needs a runtime
contract: what work moves, what work computes, what work is skipped, what work
is reordered, and how those choices are verified.

DAHA is the planner side:

```text
Input graph + model + hardware
  -> measure operation costs
  -> measure transfer costs
  -> measure CPU/GPU sampling costs
  -> derive cost vectors per batch
  -> estimate intra-batch rewrite benefit
  -> estimate inter-batch schedule benefit
  -> compare against DGL baseline
  -> save raw breakdown artifacts
```

Knight Bus should copy that shape for graph OLAP:

```text
Input projection + algorithm + RAM cap + hardware
  -> measure or estimate topology read cost
  -> measure state-vector update cost
  -> measure spill/recompute/writeback cost
  -> derive per-partition/per-frontier cost vectors
  -> choose exact-decode storage profile
  -> choose intra-partition ordering
  -> choose inter-partition schedule
  -> compare against Neo4j/GDS baseline
  -> save raw breakdown artifacts
```

SANCUS is the skip-work side. It is approximate GNN training evidence, so the
exact-OLAP transfer must be careful:

```text
SANCUS:
  Skip some broadcasts by using historical embeddings.
  Prove/argue bounded staleness and quality.

Exact Knight Bus:
  Skip work only when equality is preserved:
    settled frontier
    zero delta block
    unchanged partition
    checksum-identical sidecar
    converged residual below exact algorithm's declared stopping rule

Approximate Knight Bus:
  Skip work when bounded error is declared:
    top-k influence pruning
    stale local memory summary
    fixed-point rank vector
    lossy compressed state
```

The strongest product rule from this pass is:

```text
No hidden optimizer.

Every planner decision should be visible as:
  observed cost
  predicted cost
  selected plan
  rejected alternatives
  actual cost
  correctness or quality guard
```

New executable-spec candidates from DAHA and SANCUS:

| Spec Candidate | Contract Shape |
|---|---|
| `profile_daha_source_reference_v1` | WHEN DAHA informs a Knight Bus profile, THEN paper URL, DOI, repo URL, commit, file count, index size, planning levels, and copied-vs-inspired ideas SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_data_hardware_cost_model_v1` | WHEN a planner estimates work, THEN hardware profile, operation sample inputs, observed timings, fitted model identity, validity scope, and measured-vs-predicted delta SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_batch_operation_cost_vector_v1` | WHEN batch/partition costs are measured, THEN movement, compute, pre-transform, spill/read, writeback, proof, and baseline components SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_intra_inter_batch_plan_receipt_v1` | WHEN a profile reorders or pipelines work, THEN intra-unit plan, inter-unit schedule, dependency constraints, predicted benefit, actual benefit, and rejected plan SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_shuffle_policy_receipt_v1` | WHEN work ordering changes, THEN shuffle mode, switch boundary, seed, locality hypothesis, accuracy/correctness impact, and latency/RAM delta SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_sampling_device_comparator_v1` | WHEN CPU/GPU or resident/spill execution alternatives exist, THEN both alternatives' phase times and data-movement bytes SHALL be measured under the same workload. |
| `profile_sancus_source_reference_v1` | WHEN SANCUS informs a Knight Bus profile, THEN paper URLs, DOI, repo URL, commit, file count, index size, source-claimed communication/time/quality numbers, and exactness caveat SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_staleness_broadcast_cache_v1` | WHEN a profile reuses stale or cached state, THEN tag, source, epoch, staleness metric, cache eligibility, stored bytes, and guard threshold SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_skip_broadcast_counter_v1` | WHEN communication or work is skipped, THEN baseline count, optimized count, skipped count, per-source/per-partition decision, and same-input proof SHALL be recorded. |
| `profile_cached_vs_uncached_comm_ablation_v1` | WHEN cache-based communication avoidance is claimed, THEN cached and uncached paths SHALL run or be replayed with comparable input and output/quality diff. |
| `profile_distributed_spmm_mm_allreduce_v1` | WHEN distributed graph compute runs, THEN rank count, partition bytes, broadcast/cache decision, SpMM time, dense-compute time, all-reduce bytes/time, and output/gradient guard SHALL be recorded. |
